name: Lattice formalism for electronic occupancy sequencing
summary:
**Conversation overview**

The person is developing a formal academic paper titled "Indexing Without Prediction" concerning an ordinal lattice structure Λ identified by (n, l, k) coordinates applied to atomic configuration space. The paper's central thesis is that the lattice's order structure contributes nothing predictively beyond what the coordinates themselves supply, established through a proved information bound (Theorem 12.1 on product orders) combined with six empirical failures each characterized by mechanism. The work spans three parts: Part I refining the index itself, Part II a bracketing method for Rydberg binding energies verified on 295 interior cells, and Part III demonstrating the lattice adds no predictive uplift. Throughout the conversation the person drove the work by issuing terse directives — "run said cheap test," "proceed to the next experiment," "write it in," "make the necessary adjustments," "run the search," "recompute" — with Claude executing computations and returning findings with explicit recommendations about what warranted writing up and what did not.

The conversation progressed through a sequence of distinct research moves. Claude initially flagged three problems with the paper's framing: the word "kinetic" was unearned, prior art (Dugundji–Ugi 1973) substantially overlapped the proposed sequencing framework, and §15.4's transfer question was answerable. These led to a series of live experiments: an OH + n-alkane kinetics test showing the method fails on precision (containment degrading from 99.9% to 68.3% as step/σ fell from 5.4 to 0.7); a scheduling experiment on Λ showing adaptive measurement scheduling beats structure-only by 2.4× but that the algorithmic content is generic to posets of dimension ≥ 2; a survey of eight candidate observable channels that found the scarcity claim in §15.2 false (five of eight admit); a nuclear chart survey across nine even-Z isotopic chains from AME2020 discovering that V ≈ 11 across all chains is exactly 2S̄ₙ/Δ from nucleon pairing; a channel superposition diagnostic Σ showing every low-V case is an unresolved channel; and a systematic precision audit finding five numerical errors in tables introduced by the revision itself. The conversation ended with a blank message, which Claude treated as a prompt to continue the audit, running verification checks on the new mathematics and identifying ten internal inconsistencies in the draft — including a contradiction between §10.6 withdrawing the Ba I Σ and §10.7 reporting it, a Ni chain min-r discrepancy appearing three times with three different values, and the exclusion arithmetic in §10 no longer closing after reclassification of exclusion (ii).

Key technical findings that changed the paper's thesis: Proposition 14.1 (V > 2 exactly for any monotone sequence, approaching 2 only as one step vanishes) converts V from an empirical measure to an identity; Corollary 14.2 records that approaching the floor and obeying Rule 1 have been mutually exclusive in every case found; the closing remark of §15.4 states that the index cannot express and the method cannot predict where indexing is useful, which is the self-application of Theorem 12.1; and the Σ diagnostic requires a matched null computed at each sequence's own noise-to-step ratio rather than a fixed threshold of 1. The draft underwent progressive renaming of §15.3 withdrawn items, which by the end of the conversation had reached item 20. Appendix E was added to separate audited claims (nine items, reproducible from cited sources) from inherited-and-unaudited claims (eleven items including the 295-cell verification, all ablation costs, all closure and dimension tests, and the six mechanisms of §13), with an explicit recommendation that a referee treat the second class as unaudited given that five numerical errors were found in the audited portion alone. The most important unresolved issue requiring a complete uploaded file to fix is the contradiction around Ba I clause (ii) and the power-based replacement criterion: the count-based clause (ii) rejects ΔH_vap for the wrong reason (it has ample power; what disqualifies it is κ = 1.4), while Ba I should be reinstated (100% power against 5% alternation at nine members), so clause (ii) should be replaced with a power criterion stated at the sequence's own r.

chat_messages.text:
The construction falls out naturally enough:

A molecule with N nuclei → a fibered poset Λ⁽ᴺ⁾ = ⊔ₐ Λₐ, one copy per center, with atom a's occupancy an order ideal Iₐ ⊆ Λₐ (aufbau = downset closure). A system configuration is the tuple (I₁,…,I_N) plus a set of shared cells for bonding density. Under componentwise inclusion these tuples form a distributive lattice — but that's a product of chains, so it's free and carries no information. Sequencing is then a path in the Hasse diagram: each elementary step a covering relation where a cell (n,ℓ,k) vacates on center a and is occupied on b or in a shared cell; a mechanism is a saturated chain; a concerted step is an antichain of simultaneous covers.

Two problems before this is worth writing up.

**Nothing in it is kinetic.** Rate is barrier height on a PES over 3N−6 nuclear coordinates. Λ indexes electronic occupancy only — no geometry. Without a cost function w on Hasse edges imported from actual electronic structure, you have combinatorial enumeration of bookkeeping-legal paths, and the count of those will exceed the chemically real ones by orders of magnitude. The framework does no pruning. Decide where w comes from before the word "kinetic" earns its place.

**Prior art collision.** Dugundji & Ugi (1973) formalized exactly this: BE-matrices encoding bond-electron distribution, R-matrices as reaction operators constrained to conserve electron count, reaction sequences as paths in a metric space of BE-matrices. It's in textbooks. Your Λ⁽ᴺ⁾ is that structure re-encoded — and worse in one respect, since BE-matrices carry connectivity and the fibered poset as set up above doesn't. Any paper here has to answer what Λ buys over BE/R.

The direction I'd actually spend effort on: **Woodward–Hoffmann as an order-theoretic statement.** Correlation diagrams are already bijections between reactant and product orbital sets constrained by symmetry labels, and "forbidden" means the bijection forces an occupied→virtual crossing. If you can show a pericyclic reaction is symmetry-allowed iff a specific map Λ_react → Λ_prod is order-preserving under one of your signed orders, that's a theorem with a known finite test set, and it's the first place the lattice would do work rather than restate. It also plugs directly into the signed-order monotonicity machinery you already built.

So: do you want "kinetic" to mean rates and barriers, or just mechanism ordering — which step precedes which? The second is reachable from Λ. The first almost certainly isn't without dragging a potential energy surface in from outside.

chat_messages.text:
Your own Appendix A already answers the question I asked, and the answer is worse than "mechanism ordering only."

**Λ⁽ᴺ⁾ *is* the multi-target problem.** A molecule with N centers is N source triples and N target triples with electron conservation coupling them. Conservation is Σg ≤ Σq — a bound on a sum on both sides, outside §9.4. Appendix A already measured this: 89,864 join failures with one source, and with two sources 2.1% of pairs acquire multiple minimal upper bounds, so it isn't a join-semilattice either. My last message asserted the tuples form a distributive lattice under componentwise inclusion. That's only true if you drop conservation, and Appendix A already names what you get then: "a lattice describing configurations that cannot exist." So the structural premise of the whole sequencing idea is false, and it was falsified in your own paper before I proposed it.

**Theorem 12.1 also takes the Woodward–Hoffmann suggestion.** Symmetry labels would enter as coordinates; allowedness would then be definable from the coordinates; the order restates it. The correlation-diagram argument already *is* the theorem, in orbital-symmetry language. §13.6 is the same shape — κ collapses four monotonicities and turns out to be a restatement. I should have caught that.

**What's actually open is §15.4's third question**, and it's narrower than it looks. Transfer requires a molecular observable meeting all four of §15.2. Rate constants get two: they vary by orders of magnitude, and BEP gives a within-family monotonicity in ΔG_rxn. They fail the other two. Barriers pass through matrix elements with nodes, which is exclusion (i) — that's the same mechanism that killed your Sr I transition probabilities. And kinetic data is measured to percent, not 10⁻³ cm⁻¹, which collapses the bracket width to uselessness against the neighbour spacing.

Exclusion (iii) is the one I'd expect to bite first. "Same channel" for a reaction family means identical mechanism, identical conditions, three members measured. That's the Ti I situation: the data exists but no channel reaches three, and the method declines rather than errs.

So the cheap test, before any lattice: take one homologous SN2 or Diels–Alder series with clean kinetics, withhold a member, bracket it from its neighbours, and measure the width against the experimental error bar. If the width exceeds the spread of the series, transfer is dead and you've spent a day. No part of that test requires Λ.

The risk I'd flag plainly: "molecular kinetic sequencing" reads like the predictive program restarting under a new noun. The paper's value is that it stopped.

Ran it. Transfer is dead, and the criterion I gave you was the wrong one.

**Data.** Atkinson 2003 (ACP 3, 2233), Table 1 recommended 298 K rate coefficients for OH + n-alkanes, C1–C13. Stated overall uncertainty ±20% at 298 K for most members, ±25% for n-pentane and n-tridecane. One channel, monotone increasing in carbon number, spanning 2,359× — passes three of §15.2's four conditions outright. 11 interior cells.

**Nominal result, which is worthless.** Leave-one-out bracket coverage 11/11. That number means nothing: the published values are mutually consistent by construction, and the deductive claim is about *true* values bracketed by *true* neighbours. You never have those.

**The two numbers that matter.**

Mean bracket width is 95% of the target value. The target's own experimental interval is 82%. Ratio 1.17 — the bracket is wider than just measuring the thing. Rydberg comparison: Ba I 6s13f, width 397 cm⁻¹ on 41,251, against 10⁻³ cm⁻¹ precision. Five orders of magnitude of informativeness, gone.

Monte Carlo containment (resampling neighbours at their stated uncertainty, asking whether the published value is caught):

| C | min frac. step | step/σ | containment |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 0.54 | 5.4 | 99.9% |
| 7 | 0.20 | 2.0 | 95.1% |
| 9 | 0.13 | 1.3 | 86.3% |
| 12 | 0.07 | 0.7 | 68.3% |

Pooled 90% against a deductive claim of 100%. It degrades smoothly and predictably: containment ≈ 100% while the neighbour step exceeds ~5σ, ~95% at 2σ, ~68% at 0.7σ.

**Two side results.** Log-linear interpolation between the same two neighbours gives median error 3.2% — six times better than the measurement it's predicting, so the bracket buys nothing over the trivial estimator. And if you drop the n-alkane restriction and order all 24 alkanes by carbon number alone, 46 of 251 strictly-lower-carbon pairs (18%) violate monotonicity — neopentane C5 at 0.825 sits below propane C3 at 1.09. Rule 1's second clause is carrying the entire method, and here the channel is supplied by knowing that branching kills abstraction, not by any order structure.

**What I got wrong.** I said the test was "does the width exceed the spread of the series." It doesn't — 95% against 2,359× — so that criterion passes and discriminates nothing. The discriminating ratio is width against *measurement precision*, which I mentioned in passing and should have made the test.

**The one thing worth keeping.** This is a fifth exclusion mechanism, distinct from your four: monotone, no zeros, orders-of-magnitude variation, interior cells present, and it still fails — on precision alone. It makes §15.2's fourth condition quantitative rather than a passing remark, and gives an admission test computable before any prediction: min fractional neighbour step ≥ ~5× fractional 1σ.

Caveat worth stating in any write-up: n-alkane values are largely relative-rate chained against each other, so errors are correlated and independent-Gaussian resampling overstates the failure somewhat. The direction of the conclusion doesn't move — the C11–C13 steps are below 1σ however you correlate them.

content.text:

Abstract. The rate coefficients of the reaction of hydroxyl radicals (OH) with 12 different volatile organic compounds (VOCs), namely methane, ethane, propane, n-butane, methyl vinyl ketone (MVK), γ-terpinene, Δ3-carene, myrcene, toluene, o-xylene, m-xylene, and mesitylene, were studied in an absolute rate study in 1 atm of air between 280 and 340 K using an OH reactivity instrument with a temperature-controlled flow tube. There are few or no measurements in the literature for the important monoterpene and aromatic compounds emitted by biogenic and anthropogenic sources, although the oxidation of these species is particularly important in the formation of secondary pollutants such as ozone and particles. 

However, the result obtained in this work shows a much better agreement with the IUPAC-recommended value for room temperature (T=298 K). For aromatic compounds, no deviations from a single-exponential OH decay were observed because the presence of oxygen minimises the dissociation of the VOC–OH adduct and subsequent OH release which would cause a deviation from a single-exponential OH decay.

In this study, the temperature-dependent OH rate constants were determined for the reactions of n-alkanes (methane, ethane, propane, and n-butane) to test and validate the method and of eight other VOCs (methyl vinyl ketone, Δ3-carene, γ-terpinene, myrcene, toluene, mesitylene, m-xylene, and o-xylene) which have large biogenic or anthropogenic emission sources and for which only few or no reaction kinetic studies are available. ... The experiments were carried out using a modified laser flash photolysis–laser-induced fluorescence (LP–LIF) instrument for OH reactivity measurements.

content.text:
The experiments represent the first direct measurements of these rate constants at T > 1000 K and span a wide T-range, 797–1259 K. The present work utilized 80 optical passes corresponding to a total path length of ∼7 m. As a result of this ...

Rate constants for H-atom abstractions by OH radicals from a series of alkanes (propane, n-butane, i-butane and neo-pentane) have been measured at high temperatures with the reflected shock tube technique using multi-pass absorption spectrometric detection of OH radicals at 308 nm. The experiments represent the first direct measurements of these rate constants at T > 1000 K and span a wide T-range, 797–1259 K. The present work utilized 80 optical passes corresponding to a total path length of ∼7 m. As a result of this increased path length, the high [OH] detection sensitivity permitted pseudo-first-order analysis for unambiguously measuring the total rate constants. 

The experimental rate constants can be represented in Arrhenius form as, ... The present results have been combined with prior lower-T measurements to generate three-parameter rate expressions that adequately represent the available direct measurements (within 25%) over a wide temperature regime (250–1250 K).

A primary goal of the present study is to obtain unambiguous direct high-T measurements for OH attack on a series of small alkanes (C3–C5). The measurements can then be used in conjunction with electronic structure theory to determine CTST estimates of the rate constants and thereby make reliable extrapolations to higher-T. The present experiments have been performed with propane, n-butane, i-butane and neo-pentane using tert-butylhydroperoxide (tBH) as the OH source.

content.text:
The rate coefficients for the reactions involving OH radicals with C3–C11 alkanes in the mixed system were determined at 298 ± 1 K. The concentration curves of target alkanes and the reference compound (n-hexane) are plotted in Fig.

Abstract. Rate coefficients for the reactions of OH radicals with C3–C11 alkanes were determined using the multivariate relative-rate technique. A total of 25 relative-rate coefficients at room temperature and 24 Arrhenius expressions in the temperature range of 273–323 K were obtained. Notably, a new room temperature relative-rate coefficient for 3-methylheptane that had not been previously reported was determined, and the obtained kOH value (in units of 10−12 cm3 molec.−1 s−1) was 7.71 ± 0.35. Interestingly, whilst results for n-alkanes agreed well with available structure–activity relationship (SAR) calculations of Kwok and Atkinson (1995), Neeb (2000), Wilson et al. (2006), Jenkin et al. (2018), and McGillen et al. 

(2020), the three cycloalkanes (cyclopentane, methylcyclopentane, cyclohexane) and one branched alkane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane) were found to be less reactive than predicted by the SAR approach.

The photochemical reaction of OH ...ethylbutane, benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, p-xylene, and o-xylene was investigated at 288 and 248 K in a temperature controlled smog chamber....

In this work, we have investigated the gas phase reaction of OH with several alkanes and aromatic compounds at 288 K (sea level temperature) and 248 K (in the free troposphere this temperature corresponds to a height of approximately 5–8 km, depending on latitude and season [36]). Using n-pentane [27] and toluene [37] as reference compounds, the rate constants for the reactions of OH radicals with the 17 compounds have been obtained at 248 and 288 K. These two compounds are chosen as reference compounds, because their temperature-dependent parameters are well investigated between 220 to 350 K. Those data deliver chemical kinetic information about the temperature range below room temperature, and therefore are supplementary to the existing Arrhenius expression. 

However, more experimental research, especially with absolute measurements is needed to clarify the real reaction rate constant of OH radicals with n-heptane at low temperature. Our results for n-octane and n-nonane are consistent with previous results by Li et al. [28]. This study provides more open questions than a comprehensive understanding of gas-phase reactions of OH with n-alkanes below 290 K until precise determinations of absolute rate constants for the higher alkanes become available.

Revised: 17 November 2003 – Accepted: 18 November 2003 – Published: 22 December 2003
Abstract. The available database concerning rate constants for gas-phase reactions of the hydroxyl (OH) radical
with alkanes through early 2003 is presented over the entire temperature range for which measurements have been
made (∼180–2000 K). Measurements made using relative
rate methods are re-evaluated using recent rate data for the
reference compound (generally recommendations from this
review). In general, whenever more than one study has been
carried out over an overlapping temperature range, recommended rate constants or temperature-dependent rate expressions are presented. The recommended 298 K rate constants,
temperature-dependent parameters, and temperature ranges
over which these recommendations are applicable are listed
in Table 1.
1 Introduction
Large quantities of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) are
emitted into the atmosphere from anthropogenic and biogenic sources, and a large number of VOCs are present in
ambient air (including those formed in situ from the atmospheric reactions of other VOCs). In the troposphere, VOCs
can be transformed by photolysis (at wavelengths ≥290 nm),
reaction with hydroxyl (OH) radicals (mainly during daylight
hours), reaction with nitrate (NO3) radicals (during evening
and nighttime hours), and reaction with ozone (O3) (Atkinson, 2000).
Alkanes are an important class of VOCs (Calvert et al.,
2002) which in the atmosphere react with OH radicals and,
to a lesser extent, with NO3 radicals (Atkinson, 2000).
Rate constants for the gas-phase reactions of OH radicals
with alkanes have been periodically reviewed and evaluated
(Atkinson, 1986, 1989, 1994, 1997), and the reactions of OH
Correspondence to: R. Atkinson
(ratkins@mail.ucr.edu)
radicals with ≤C4 alkanes are included in the ongoing NASA
(2003) and IUPAC (2003) data evaluations (which are now
only available on the World Wide Web, at the locations given
in NASA (2003) and IUPAC, 2003). This review and evaluation continues the previous reviews and evaluations of Atkinson (1986, 1989, 1994, 1997), and employs the same general
format.
For each alkane and cycloalkane for which experimental
kinetic data are available in the readily accessible literature,
these rate constants are listed. In the table associated with
each reaction, the experimental techniques used are denoted
by the abbreviations listed in Table 2. For example, use of
a flash photolysis system to generate OH radicals with resonance fluorescence monitoring of OH radicals is denoted by
PF-RF. When relative rate methods (denoted in the “Technique” column by “RR”) were used, the rate constant for the
reference compound from the most recent review and evaluation is used to re-evaluate the rate constant for the alkane
in question (which therefore may be different from that cited
in the original publication). For relative rate studies, the rate
constant used for the reference reaction to place the measured
rate constant ratio(s) on an absolute basis is noted, and is that
recommended from this evaluation (including the rate constants derived in this review and evaluation for the reactions
of OH radicals with H2 and CO), unless noted otherwise.
For absolute rate studies, the temperature-dependent rate
expressions are also given (if cited), either as the Arrhenius expression k=Ae−B/T (in which case no entry is given
in the column labeled n) or as the three-parameter expression k=AT n
e

expression k=CT ne

import numpy as np, itertools
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)

# Atkinson (2003) ACP 3, 2233 -- Table 1 recommended 298 K rate constants
# units 1e-12 cm3 molecule-1 s-1
nalk = [(1,0.00640,.20),(2,0.248,.20),(3,1.09,.20),(4,2.36,.20),(5,3.80,.25),
        (6,5.20,.20),(7,6.76,.20),(8,8.11,.20),(9,9.70,.20),(10,11.0,.20),
        (11,12.3,.20),(12,13.2,.20),(13,15.1,.25)]
C = np.array([a for a,b,c in nalk]); K = np.array([b for a,b,c in nalk]); U = np.array([c for a,b,c in nalk])

print("=== A. n-alkane channel: leave-one-out deductive bracket ===")
print(" C   k_meas    bracket lo-hi        width   width/k  exp 2u interval width/k")
cov=0; rows=[]
for i in range(1,len(C)-1):
    lo,hi = K[i-1],K[i+1]                       # monotone increasing in C
    w = hi-lo; ok = lo<=K[i]<=hi; cov+=ok
    expw = 2*U[i]*K[i]*2                        # full +/-u interval width
    rows.append((C[i],K[i],lo,hi,w,w/K[i],expw/K[i]))
    print(f"{C[i]:3d} {K[i]:7.3f}  [{lo:7.3f},{hi:7.3f}]  {w:7.3f}  {w/K[i]:6.2f}   {expw/K[i]:6.2f}   {'OK' if ok else 'FAIL'}")
print(f"coverage {cov}/{len(C)-2}")
mw = np.mean([r[5] for r in rows]); me = np.mean([r[6] for r in rows])
print(f"mean bracket width  = {mw*100:.0f}% of value")
print(f"mean exp. interval  = {me*100:.0f}% of value   ratio = {mw/me:.2f}")
print(f"series total spread = {K.max()/K.min():.0f}x  ({K.max()-K.min():.2f} units)")

print("\n=== B. does the bracket survive measurement error? ===")
# treat published k as truth +/- stated u; resample 'measured' neighbours, ask if truth is contained
N=200000; fails=np.zeros(len(C))
for t in range(N):
    m = K*(1+rng.normal(0,U/2,len(K)))   # stated u read as 2-sigma
    for i in range(1,len(C)-1):
        if not (min(m[i-1],m[i+1])<=K[i]<=max(m[i-1],m[i+1])): fails[i]+=1
for i in range(1,len(C)-1):
    print(f" C{C[i]:<3d} containment {100*(1-fails[i]/N):5.1f}%")
print(f" pooled containment {100*(1-fails.sum()/(N*(len(C)-2))):.1f}%   (deductive claim: 100%)")

print("\n=== C. what a zero-effort baseline gets ===")
# log-linear interpolation between the same two neighbours = the Ritz analogue
errs=[]
for i in range(1,len(C)-1):
    p = np.exp(np.interp(C[i],[C[i-1],C[i+1]],[np.log(K[i-1]),np.log(K[i+1])]))
    errs.append(abs(p-K[i])/K[i])
print(f" log-interp point estimate: median |err| {100*np.median(errs):.1f}%, max {100*max(errs):.1f}%")
print(f" vs stated experimental uncertainty on the same cells: {100*np.mean(U[1:-1]):.0f}%")

print("\n=== D. channel discipline: order by carbon number alone ===")
allk = [(1,'methane',.00640),(2,'ethane',.248),(3,'propane',1.09),
 (4,'n-butane',2.36),(4,'2-methylpropane',2.12),
 (5,'n-pentane',3.80),(5,'2-methylbutane',3.6),(5,'neopentane',0.825),
 (6,'n-hexane',5.20),(6,'2-methylpentane',5.2),(6,'3-methylpentane',5.2),
 (6,'2,2-dimethylbutane',2.23),(6,'2,3-dimethylbutane',5.78),
 (7,'n-heptane',6.76),(7,'2,4-dimethylpentane',4.8),(7,'2,2,3-trimethylbutane',3.81),
 (8,'n-octane',8.11),(8,'2,2,4-trimethylpentane',3.34),(8,'2,3,4-trimethylpentane',6.6),
 (8,'2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane',0.972),
 (9,'n-nonane',9.70),(9,'3,3-diethylpentane',4.8),
 (10,'n-decane',11.0),(10,'3,4-diethylhexane',6.9)]
viol=[(a,b) for a,b in itertools.combinations(allk,2) if a[0]<b[0] and a[2]>b[2]]
comp=[(a,b) for a,b in itertools.combinations(allk,2) if a[0]<b[0]]
print(f" strictly-lower-carbon pairs: {len(comp)}, monotonicity violations: {len(viol)} ({100*len(viol)/len(comp):.0f}%)")
for a,b in viol[:5]: print(f"   {a[1]}(C{a[0]}) {a[2]} > {b[1]}(C{b[0]}) {b[2]}")
print(f"   ... worst: neopentane C5 0.825 < propane C3 1.09")

summaries.summary: Scrutinizing hydrocarbon coverage metrics and bracket width calculations.
Evaluated transfer criterion validity and identified measurement precision threshold.

content.text:
Ran it. Transfer is dead, and the criterion I gave you was the wrong one.

**Data.** Atkinson 2003 (ACP 3, 2233), Table 1 recommended 298 K rate coefficients for OH + n-alkanes, C1–C13. Stated overall uncertainty ±20% at 298 K for most members, ±25% for n-pentane and n-tridecane. One channel, monotone increasing in carbon number, spanning 2,359× — passes three of §15.2's four conditions outright. 11 interior cells.

**Nominal result, which is worthless.** Leave-one-out bracket coverage 11/11. That number means nothing: the published values are mutually consistent by construction, and the deductive claim is about *true* values bracketed by *true* neighbours. You never have those.

**The two numbers that matter.**

Mean bracket width is 95% of the target value. The target's own experimental interval is 82%. Ratio 1.17 — the bracket is wider than just measuring the thing. Rydberg comparison: Ba I 6s13f, width 397 cm⁻¹ on 41,251, against 10⁻³ cm⁻¹ precision. Five orders of magnitude of informativeness, gone.

Monte Carlo containment (resampling neighbours at their stated uncertainty, asking whether the published value is caught):

| C | min frac. step | step/σ | containment |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 0.54 | 5.4 | 99.9% |
| 7 | 0.20 | 2.0 | 95.1% |
| 9 | 0.13 | 1.3 | 86.3% |
| 12 | 0.07 | 0.7 | 68.3% |

Pooled 90% against a deductive claim of 100%. It degrades smoothly and predictably: containment ≈ 100% while the neighbour step exceeds ~5σ, ~95% at 2σ, ~68% at 0.7σ.

**Two side results.** Log-linear interpolation between the same two neighbours gives median error 3.2% — six times better than the measurement it's predicting, so the bracket buys nothing over the trivial estimator. And if you drop the n-alkane restriction and order all 24 alkanes by carbon number alone, 46 of 251 strictly-lower-carbon pairs (18%) violate monotonicity — neopentane C5 at 0.825 sits below propane C3 at 1.09. Rule 1's second clause is carrying the entire method, and here the channel is supplied by knowing that branching kills abstraction, not by any order structure.

**What I got wrong.** I said the test was "does the width exceed the spread of the series." It doesn't — 95% against 2,359× — so that criterion passes and discriminates nothing. The discriminating ratio is width against *measurement precision*, which I mentioned in passing and should have made the test.

**The one thing worth keeping.** This is a fifth exclusion mechanism, distinct from your four: monotone, no zeros, orders-of-magnitude variation, interior cells present, and it still fails — on precision alone. It makes §15.2's fourth condition quantitative rather than a passing remark, and gives an admission test computable before any prediction: min fractional neighbour step ≥ ~5× fractional 1σ.

Caveat worth stating in any write-up: n-alkane values are largely relative-rate chained against each other, so errors are correlated and independent-Gaussian resampling overstates the failure somewhat. The direction of the conclusion doesn't move — the C11–C13 steps are below 1σ however you correlate them.

chat_messages.text:
Six, honestly ranked. But first the thing today's result already gives you, because it changes which paths are worth taking.

**The exclusions collapse.** (ii) flatness and (v) precision are not two mechanisms. Flatness shrinks the numerator, precision inflates the denominator, and only step/σ appears in the containment curve. (iii) — fewer than three members in a channel — is the degenerate case where no step exists at all. Three of your exclusions are one number with a threshold near 5. That's a simplification of §15.2 you can state and defend, and it's cheap to write up. Only (i), the node/matrix-element exclusion, is structurally different, because it breaks monotonicity rather than resolution.

---

**1. Retarget §15.4's third question at molecular spectroscopy, not kinetics.** The admission test tells you exactly where to look: observables with absurd precision and coarse steps. Rotational constants (10⁻⁵–10⁻⁶ relative), PFI-ZEKE ionization energies (~1 cm⁻¹ on ~10⁵), vibrational fundamentals. Homologous series and isotopologue series both give you channels with three-plus members. The honest risk is that the same series that give you precision also asymptote — n-alkane IEs converge toward the polymer limit — so you'd be trading (v) against (ii) along the same axis. Characterizing that trade-off *is* the paper. One dataset, a day or two. Highest value per hour of anything on this list.

**2. Write the audit paper and stop there.** Rule 1, the conditions, the collapsed exclusion set, the admission test, and three worked failures — Sr I transition probabilities, Ti I channel starvation, OH+alkane precision. A method that declines correctly on three off-domain observables is a real result, and it's the only framing where the negative findings are the contribution rather than the wreckage. This is what I'd actually publish.

**3. Measurement scheduling on the poset.** The one place I can see Λ doing work rather than restating. Brackets propagate along chains; in a genuine three-coordinate partial order a cell sits on several, so "which unmeasured cell tightens the most brackets" is a coverage problem whose answer depends on the Hasse structure and not on any lookup table. Modest, but it's not a recoding. Worth a section if it works, worth abandoning fast if the optimum turns out to be bisection.

Ran it. There's one finding worth keeping, and it isn't the one path 3 was proposing.

**Setup.** Λ built as the 118 ground-state (n,ℓ,k) cells over the standard filling order, componentwise order. Comparability density 0.542, one minimal element (1s¹), three maximal (5f¹⁴, 6d¹⁰, 7p⁶). Objective: mean bracket width over unmeasured cells, unbracketed scored as full range. Four monotone test surfaces (linear, steep-in-n, saturating, k-dominant), normalised.

**The null control fires cleanly.** On a 118-cell chain with endpoints seeded, bisection equals the myopic oracle to four decimals at every budget — 1.00× at B = 8, 16, 32, 48. So in 1D there is nothing here, exactly as you suspected.

**On Λ it does not collapse.**

| B | static (structure-only) | adaptive-midpoint | oracle |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16 | 0.3505 | 0.3393 | 0.1405 |
| 32 | 0.3206 | 0.1788 | 0.0742 |
| 48 | 0.2499 | 0.1046 | 0.0498 |

Three things in that table. Static structure-only scheduling *plateaus and regresses* — 0.3062 at B=24, 0.3206 at B=32 — because "central" cells in a partial order are incomparable to most of what remains. Adaptive-midpoint (implementable; uses only measured values, assumes each unmeasured cell sits at its bracket midpoint) pulls away as budget grows: 1.03× → 2.39× over static. And nobody reaches the oracle; a ~2× gap persists.

The optimal schedule is also **data-dependent**: optimal 16-cell schedules for the four surfaces overlap in only 4–7 cells, and applying one surface's schedule to another costs up to 2.3×. So there is no precomputable "optimal measurement schedule for Λ."

**And here's what kills it as a Λ result.** I ran the same experiment on a plain 5×5×5 box poset and a random 3-coordinate cloud at matched size:

| poset | density | adapt gain @48 | gap to oracle |
|---|---|---|---|
| Λ | 0.542 | 2.39× | 2.10× |
| 5×5×5 box | 0.391 | 2.11× | 1.91× |
| random cloud | 0.298 | 1.48× | 1.43× |

Same curve, same signs, magnitude tracking comparability density and nothing else. This is a fact about graded posets of dimension ≥ 2, with Λ as an unremarkable instance. Writing it as a finding about the periodic table would be the restatement failure again, one level up.

**The one Λ-specific thing.** Λ has no top element. Its three maximal cells are 5f¹⁴, 6d¹⁰, 7p⁶, sitting above 91, 81 and 49 of the other 117 cells respectively, and 46 cells are covered by exactly one of them. So two-sided bracketing anywhere in the table is gated on measuring the termini of the 5f, 6d and 7p blocks — precisely the region where experimental data is worst and in places nonexistent. That's a concrete, checkable structural obstruction, and it explains why bracketedness rather than width is the binding constraint at low budget. It's a paragraph, not a section.

**Caveats I'd state in any write-up.** The oracle sees the true values, so part of that 2× gap measures cheating rather than headroom. Surfaces are synthetic. And the objective ignores measurement error entirely — which matters, because of the following.

**The synthesis, which I think is the actual output of today.** A 2× reduction in bracket width is arithmetically identical to a 2× improvement in step/σ. Last session's containment curve and this session's scheduling objective are the same quantity approached from opposite ends: precision is the measurement-side lever on step/σ, scheduling is the design-side lever. Collapsing exclusions (ii), (iii) and (v) into one ratio, as we did, and now finding that the scheduling optimum is also that ratio, means the paper has one free parameter left. That's a real simplification and it's worth stating as such.

**Recommendation.** Not a section. Half a subsection inside path 2: the admission test has two knobs, here is the poset-side one, here is the honest note that its algorithmic content is generic to dimension ≥ 2, and here is the 5f/6d/7p obstruction, which is yours. Then go do path 1, where the precision knob might actually get you above threshold.

import numpy as np, itertools
rng=np.random.default_rng(1)
SUB=[(1,0),(2,0),(2,1),(3,0),(3,1),(4,0),(3,2),(4,1),(5,0),(4,2),(5,1),
     (6,0),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1),(7,0),(5,3),(6,2),(7,1)]
cells=sorted({(n,l,k) for (n,l) in SUB for k in range(1,2*(2*l+1)+1)})
A=np.array(cells); N=len(cells)
le=np.all(A[:,None,:]<=A[None,:,:],axis=2); np.fill_diagonal(le,True)
DOWN=[np.where(le[:,i])[0] for i in range(N)]   # cells <= i
UP  =[np.where(le[i,:])[0] for i in range(N)]   # cells >= i

def truths():
    n,l,k=A[:,0],A[:,1],A[:,2]
    t={}
    t['linear']   = 1.0*n+1.0*l+0.3*k
    t['steep-n']  = 2.0**n + l + 0.2*k
    t['saturating']=(1-np.exp(-0.6*n))*10 + l + 0.15*k
    t['k-dominant']=0.2*n+0.2*l+1.0*k
    for key in t:
        v=t[key]; t[key]=(v-v.min())/(v.max()-v.min())
    return t
T=truths()

def widths(meas, f):
    """meas: boolean array. returns per-cell width, np.nan if unbracketed one side"""
    w=np.zeros(N); M=np.where(meas)[0]
    for i in range(N):
        if meas[i]: w[i]=0.0; continue
        below=[f[j] for j in DOWN[i] if meas[j]]
        above=[f[j] for j in UP[i]   if meas[j]]
        if below and above: w[i]=min(above)-max(below)
        else: w[i]=1.0                      # unbracketed = full normalised range
    return w

def score(meas,f):
    w=widths(meas,f); un=~meas
    return w[un].mean() if un.any() else 0.0

# ---------------- strategies ----------------
def s_random(B,f,seed):
    r=np.random.default_rng(seed); return r.choice(N,B,replace=False)

def s_extremes_then_random(B,f,seed):
    # measure minimal + maximal elements first (guarantee bracketing), then random
    ext=[i for i in range(N) if le[i].sum()==1 or le[:,i].sum()==1]
    r=np.random.default_rng(seed); rest=[i for i in range(N) if i not in ext]
    return np.array(ext+list(r.choice(rest,max(0,B-len(ext)),replace=False)))[:B]

def s_product(B,f,seed):
    """structure-only: greedily pick argmax |unmeasured up| * |unmeasured down|"""
    meas=np.zeros(N,bool); pick=[]
    for _ in range(B):
        best,bi=-1,None
        for i in range(N):
            if meas[i]: continue
            d=sum(1 for j in DOWN[i] if not meas[j]); u=sum(1 for j in UP[i] if not meas[j])
            v=d*u
            if v>best: best,bi=v,i
        meas[bi]=True; pick.append(bi)
    return np.array(pick)

def s_chainbisect(B,f,seed):
    """decompose into chains (greedy longest-chain peeling), bisect each in turn"""
    remaining=set(range(N)); chains=[]
    while remaining:
        sub=sorted(remaining)
        best=[]
        # longest chain in remaining by DP over topological (sum) order
        order=sorted(sub,key=lambda i:A[i].sum())
        L={i:[i] for i in order}
        for i in order:
            for j in order:
                if j!=i and le[j,i] and j in L and len(L[j])+1>len(L[i]): L[i]=L[j]+[i]
        best=max((L[i] for i in order),key=len)
        chains.append(best); remaining-=set(best)
    chains.sort(key=len,reverse=True)
    # round-robin bisection within chains
    picks=[]; segs={ci:[(0,len(c)-1)] for ci,c in enumerate(chains)}
    done=set()
    while len(picks)<B:
        progressed=False
        for ci,c in enumerate(chains):
            if len(picks)>=B: break
            s=segs[ci]
            if not s: continue
            s.sort(key=lambda ab: ab[1]-ab[0], reverse=True)
            a,b=s.pop(0)
            if b<a: continue
            m=(a+b)//2
            if c[m] not in done:
                picks.append(c[m]); done.add(c[m]); progressed=True
            if m-1>=a: s.append((a,m-1))
            if m+1<=b: s.append((m+1,b))
        if not progressed: break
    while len(picks)<B:
        r=[i for i in range(N) if i not in done]; picks.append(r[0]); done.add(r[0])
    return np.array(picks[:B])

def s_greedy_oracle(B,f,seed):
    """adaptive, sees true values: myopic minimiser of mean width. Upper bound."""
    meas=np.zeros(N,bool); pick=[]
    for _ in range(B):
        best,bi=1e9,None
        for i in range(N):
            if meas[i]: continue
            meas[i]=True; v=score(meas,f); meas[i]=False
            if v<best: best,bi=v,i
        meas[bi]=True; pick.append(bi)
    return np.array(pick)

STRATS={'random':s_random,'extremes+random':s_extremes_then_random,
        'chain-bisect':s_chainbisect,'poset-product':s_product,
        'greedy-oracle(adaptive)':s_greedy_oracle}

BUD=[4,8,12,16,24,32]
print(f"{'strategy':26s}"+"".join(f"{b:>9d}" for b in BUD))
res={}
for name,fn in STRATS.items():
    row=[]
    for B in BUD:
        vals=[]
        for tname,f in T.items():
            reps=8 if name in ('random','extremes+random') else 1
            for r in range(reps):
                sel=fn(B,f,seed=100+r)
                meas=np.zeros(N,bool); meas[sel]=True
                vals.append(score(meas,f))
        row.append(np.mean(vals))
    res[name]=row
    print(f"{name:26s}"+"".join(f"{v:9.4f}" for v in row))
np.save('res.npy',res,allow_pickle=True)
EOF

import numpy as np
exec(open('sched.py').read().split('# ---------------- strategies')[0])
def widths(meas,f):
    w=np.zeros(N)
    for i in range(N):
        if meas[i]: continue
        b=[f[j] for j in DOWN[i] if meas[j]]; a=[f[j] for j in UP[i] if meas[j]]
        w[i]=(min(a)-max(b)) if (b and a) else 1.0
    return w
def score(m,f): un=~m; return widths(m,f)[un].mean()
ext=[i for i in range(N) if le[i].sum()==1 or le[:,i].sum()==1]

def oracle(B,f):
    m=np.zeros(N,bool)
    for _ in range(B):
        best,bi=1e9,None
        for i in range(N):
            if m[i]: continue
            m[i]=True; v=score(m,f); m[i]=False
            if v<best: best,bi=v,i
        m[bi]=True
    return m
def static_product(B):
    m=np.zeros(N,bool); m[ext]=True
    while m.sum()<B:
        best,bi=-1,None
        for i in range(N):
            if m[i]: continue
            d=sum(1 for j in DOWN[i] if not m[j]); u=sum(1 for j in UP[i] if not m[j])
            if d*u>best: best,bi=d*u,i
        m[bi]=True
    return m
def adaptive_mid(B,f):
    """implementable: uses ONLY measured values. Assumes an unmeasured cell sits at
       the midpoint of its current bracket, picks the cell minimising resulting mean width."""
    m=np.zeros(N,bool); m[ext]=True
    while m.sum()<B:
        w=widths(m,f)
        best,bi=1e9,None
        for i in range(N):
            if m[i]: continue
            b=[f[j] for j in DOWN[i] if m[j]]; a=[f[j] for j in UP[i] if m[j]]
            guess=(max(b)+min(a))/2 if (b and a) else 0.5
            fg=f.copy(); fg[i]=guess; m[i]=True
            v=score(m,fg); m[i]=False
            if v<best: best,bi=v,i
        m[bi]=True
    return m

print("=== POSET (118 cells, comparability 0.542) ===")
print(f"{'B':>4} {'static-product':>15} {'adaptive-midpoint':>19} {'oracle':>9} {'adapt gain':>11}")
for B in [8,12,16,24,32,48]:
    sp=np.mean([score(static_product(B),f) for f in T.values()])
    ad=np.mean([score(adaptive_mid(B,f),f) for f in T.values()])
    orc=np.mean([score(oracle(B,f),f) for f in T.values()])
    print(f"{B:4d} {sp:15.4f} {ad:19.4f} {orc:9.4f} {sp/ad:10.2f}x")

print("\n=== CHAIN control (118 cells, endpoints seeded) ===")
Nc=118; fc=np.linspace(0,1,Nc)
def cw(m,f):
    w=np.zeros(Nc)
    for i in range(Nc):
        if m[i]: continue
        b=[f[j] for j in range(i) if m[j]]; a=[f[j] for j in range(i+1,Nc) if m[j]]
        w[i]=(min(a)-max(b)) if (b and a) else 1.0
    return w
def cs(m,f): return cw(m,f)[~m].mean()
def cbis(B):
    m=np.zeros(Nc,bool); m[0]=m[Nc-1]=True; segs=[(1,Nc-2)]
    while m.sum()<B and segs:
        segs.sort(key=lambda ab:ab[1]-ab[0],reverse=True); a,b=segs.pop(0)
        if b<a: continue
        mid=(a+b)//2; m[mid]=True
        if mid-1>=a: segs.append((a,mid-1))
        if mid+1<=b: segs.append((mid+1,b))
    return m
def corc(B):
    m=np.zeros(Nc,bool)
    for _ in range(B):
        best,bi=1e9,None
        for i in range(Nc):
            if m[i]: continue
            m[i]=True; v=cs(m,fc); m[i]=False
            if v<best: best,bi=v,i
        m[bi]=True
    return m
print(f"{'B':>4} {'bisection':>11} {'oracle':>9} {'ratio':>8}")
for B in [8,16,32,48]:
    b=cs(cbis(B),fc); o=cs(corc(B),fc)
    print(f"{B:4d} {b:11.4f} {o:9.4f} {b/o:7.2f}x")

import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(3)
def build(A):
    N=len(A); le=np.all(A[:,None,:]<=A[None,:,:],axis=2); np.fill_diagonal(le,True)
    return N,le,[np.where(le[:,i])[0] for i in range(N)],[np.where(le[i,:])[0] for i in range(N)]
def make_T(A):
    n,l,k=A[:,0],A[:,1],A[:,2]; t={}
    t['linear']=1.0*n+1.0*l+0.3*k; t['steep']=2.0**n+l+0.2*k
    t['sat']=(1-np.exp(-0.6*n))*10+l+0.15*k; t['kdom']=0.2*n+0.2*l+1.0*k
    return {a:(v-v.min())/(v.max()-v.min()) for a,v in t.items()}
def run(A,label):
    N,le,DOWN,UP=build(A); T=make_T(A)
    ext=[i for i in range(N) if le[i].sum()==1 or le[:,i].sum()==1]
    dens=(le|le.T).sum()-N; dens/= N*(N-1)
    def widths(m,f):
        w=np.zeros(N)
        for i in range(N):
            if m[i]: continue
            b=[f[j] for j in DOWN[i] if m[j]]; a=[f[j] for j in UP[i] if m[j]]
            w[i]=(min(a)-max(b)) if (b and a) else 1.0
        return w
    def sc(m,f): return widths(m,f)[~m].mean()
    def static(B):
        m=np.zeros(N,bool); m[ext[:B]]=True
        while m.sum()<B:
            best,bi=-1,None
            for i in range(N):
                if m[i]: continue
                d=sum(1 for j in DOWN[i] if not m[j]); u=sum(1 for j in UP[i] if not m[j])
                if d*u>best: best,bi=d*u,i
            m[bi]=True
        return m
    def adap(B,f):
        m=np.zeros(N,bool); m[ext[:B]]=True
        while m.sum()<B:
            best,bi=1e9,None
            for i in range(N):
                if m[i]: continue
                b=[f[j] for j in DOWN[i] if m[j]]; a=[f[j] for j in UP[i] if m[j]]
                g=(max(b)+min(a))/2 if (b and a) else 0.5
                fg=f.copy(); fg[i]=g; m[i]=True; v=sc(m,fg); m[i]=False
                if v<best: best,bi=v,i
            m[bi]=True
        return m
    def orc(B,f):
        m=np.zeros(N,bool)
        for _ in range(B):
            best,bi=1e9,None
            for i in range(N):
                if m[i]: continue
                m[i]=True; v=sc(m,f); m[i]=False
                if v<best: best,bi=v,i
            m[bi]=True
        return m
    out=[]
    for B in [16,32,48]:
        s=np.mean([sc(static(B),f) for f in T.values()])
        a=np.mean([sc(adap(B,f),f) for f in T.values()])
        o=np.mean([sc(orc(B,f),f) for f in T.values()])
        out.append((B,s,a,o,s/a,a/o))
    print(f"\n{label}  |P|={N} density={dens:.3f} maximal={sum(1 for i in range(N) if le[i].sum()==1)}")
    print(f"{'B':>4}{'static':>9}{'adaptive':>10}{'oracle':>9}{'adapt gain':>12}{'gap to orc':>12}")
    for B,s,a,o,g1,g2 in out: print(f"{B:4d}{s:9.4f}{a:10.4f}{o:9.4f}{g1:11.2f}x{g2:11.2f}x")

SUB=[(1,0),(2,0),(2,1),(3,0),(3,1),(4,0),(3,2),(4,1),(5,0),(4,2),(5,1),
     (6,0),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1),(7,0),(5,3),(6,2),(7,1)]
run(np.array(sorted({(n,l,k) for (n,l) in SUB for k in range(1,2*(2*l+1)+1)})),"Lambda (real)")
# plain 3D box with matched size
run(np.array([(a,b,c) for a in range(1,6) for b in range(1,6) for c in range(1,6)])[:118],"3D box 5x5x5")
# random 3-coordinate cloud, matched N
run(rng.integers(1,15,size=(118,3)),"random 3-coord cloud")

        m=np.zeros(N,bool); m[ext[:B]]=True
        while m.sum()<B:
            best,bi=1e9,None
            for i in range(N):
                if m[i]: continue
                b=[f[j] for j in DOWN[i] if m[j]]; a=[f[j] for j in UP[i] if m[j]]
                g=(max(b)+min(a))/2 if (b and a) else 0.5
                fg=f.copy(); fg[i]=g; m[i]=True; v=sc(m,fg); m[i]=False
                if v<best: best,bi=v,i
            m[bi]=True
        return m
    def orc(B,f):
        m=np.zeros(N,bool)
        for _ in range(B):
            best,bi=1e9,None
            for i in range(N):
                if m[i]: continue
                m[i]=True; v=sc(m,f); m[i]=False
                if v<best: best,bi=v,i
            m[bi]=True
        return m
    out=[]
    for B in [16,32,48]:
        s=np.mean([sc(static(B),f) for f in T.values()])
        a=np.mean([sc(adap(B,f),f) for f in T.values()])
        o=np.mean([sc(orc(B,f),f) for f in T.values()])
        out.append((B,s,a,o,s/a,a/o))
    print(f"\n{label}  |P|={N} density={dens:.3f} maximal={sum(1 for i in range(N) if le[i].sum()==1)}")
    print(f"{'B':>4}{'static':>9}{'adaptive':>10}{'oracle':>9}{'adapt gain':>12}{'gap to orc':>12}")
    for B,s,a,o,g1,g2 in out: print(f"{B:4d}{s:9.4f}{a:10.4f}{o:9.4f}{g1:11.2f}x{g2:11.2f}x")

content.text:
Ran it. There's one finding worth keeping, and it isn't the one path 3 was proposing.

**Setup.** Λ built as the 118 ground-state (n,ℓ,k) cells over the standard filling order, componentwise order. Comparability density 0.542, one minimal element (1s¹), three maximal (5f¹⁴, 6d¹⁰, 7p⁶). Objective: mean bracket width over unmeasured cells, unbracketed scored as full range. Four monotone test surfaces (linear, steep-in-n, saturating, k-dominant), normalised.

**The null control fires cleanly.** On a 118-cell chain with endpoints seeded, bisection equals the myopic oracle to four decimals at every budget — 1.00× at B = 8, 16, 32, 48. So in 1D there is nothing here, exactly as you suspected.

**On Λ it does not collapse.**

| B | static (structure-only) | adaptive-midpoint | oracle |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16 | 0.3505 | 0.3393 | 0.1405 |
| 32 | 0.3206 | 0.1788 | 0.0742 |
| 48 | 0.2499 | 0.1046 | 0.0498 |

Three things in that table. Static structure-only scheduling *plateaus and regresses* — 0.3062 at B=24, 0.3206 at B=32 — because "central" cells in a partial order are incomparable to most of what remains. Adaptive-midpoint (implementable; uses only measured values, assumes each unmeasured cell sits at its bracket midpoint) pulls away as budget grows: 1.03× → 2.39× over static. And nobody reaches the oracle; a ~2× gap persists.

The optimal schedule is also **data-dependent**: optimal 16-cell schedules for the four surfaces overlap in only 4–7 cells, and applying one surface's schedule to another costs up to 2.3×. So there is no precomputable "optimal measurement schedule for Λ."

**And here's what kills it as a Λ result.** I ran the same experiment on a plain 5×5×5 box poset and a random 3-coordinate cloud at matched size:

| poset | density | adapt gain @48 | gap to oracle |
|---|---|---|---|
| Λ | 0.542 | 2.39× | 2.10× |
| 5×5×5 box | 0.391 | 2.11× | 1.91× |
| random cloud | 0.298 | 1.48× | 1.43× |

Same curve, same signs, magnitude tracking comparability density and nothing else. This is a fact about graded posets of dimension ≥ 2, with Λ as an unremarkable instance. Writing it as a finding about the periodic table would be the restatement failure again, one level up.

**The one Λ-specific thing.** Λ has no top element. Its three maximal cells are 5f¹⁴, 6d¹⁰, 7p⁶, sitting above 91, 81 and 49 of the other 117 cells respectively, and 46 cells are covered by exactly one of them. So two-sided bracketing anywhere in the table is gated on measuring the termini of the 5f, 6d and 7p blocks — precisely the region where experimental data is worst and in places nonexistent. That's a concrete, checkable structural obstruction, and it explains why bracketedness rather than width is the binding constraint at low budget. It's a paragraph, not a section.

**Caveats I'd state in any write-up.** The oracle sees the true values, so part of that 2× gap measures cheating rather than headroom. Surfaces are synthetic. And the objective ignores measurement error entirely — which matters, because of the following.

**The synthesis, which I think is the actual output of today.** A 2× reduction in bracket width is arithmetically identical to a 2× improvement in step/σ. Last session's containment curve and this session's scheduling objective are the same quantity approached from opposite ends: precision is the measurement-side lever on step/σ, scheduling is the design-side lever. Collapsing exclusions (ii), (iii) and (v) into one ratio, as we did, and now finding that the scheduling optimum is also that ratio, means the paper has one free parameter left. That's a real simplification and it's worth stating as such.

**Recommendation.** Not a section. Half a subsection inside path 2: the admission test has two knobs, here is the poset-side one, here is the honest note that its algorithmic content is generic to dimension ≥ 2, and here is the 5f/6d/7p obstruction, which is yours. Then go do path 1, where the precision knob might actually get you above threshold.

This is the audit paper, and it works. The reframe did what it needed to: the negative results are now the contribution rather than the wreckage, §15.3 and Appendix D are unusually honest for the genre, and the anchoring disclosure in §11.1 and Appendix D is the kind of thing most authors bury. Keep both prominent. Reviews below, ordered by severity.

**1. Theorem 12.1 doesn't support the weight §12 puts on it.** "Definable from the coordinates" is an information-theoretic statement. "Can restate them but never exceed them" is an estimation-theoretic one, and it doesn't follow. Deterministic functions of the inputs routinely improve finite-sample learners — that's what feature engineering is. Your six mechanisms are strong empirical evidence, but as written the paper claims a theorem forbids uplift when what you have is a theorem forbidding *new information* plus six failed attempts at *estimation* uplift. A referee in statistics will hit this immediately. The fix is cheap: state Theorem 12.1 as bounding information, then say explicitly that estimation uplift remains logically possible and that §13 reports six attempts to find it, each failing for a reason that generalises. That's still your thesis, and it survives contact.

**2. §13.2 and §14 assign opposite value to the same object.** §13.2 dismisses comparability-ordering because it is "a theorem given monotonicity, not an empirical finding." §14 celebrates bracketing because it is "an entailment: given that the property is monotone." Same epistemic status, opposite verdicts. The real distinction is whether a coordinate-based method reproduces the output — a positive-weight sum reproduces the ordering (§13.3) but does not produce a guaranteed interval. Say that. As written the two sections read as inconsistent, and it's your central claim.

**3. Exclusion (ii)'s mechanism is misdiagnosed, and your own number is the evidence.** "A constant is not monotone" predicts 50% bracket coverage: if the true values are flat and the neighbours carry iid noise, the bracket catches the target exactly when the two neighbours straddle it. You report 35.3%. That's fifteen points below the floor your own stated mechanism allows, which means something systematic is running against the assumed direction — worth chasing before publication, because as it stands the number contradicts the explanation attached to it.

The mechanism you actually described in that paragraph is resolution, not monotonicity: steps of ~0.5% against 1.6% noise. That ratio — fractional neighbour step over fractional measurement error — is the whole thing, and it generates a one-parameter curve:

| step/σ | containment |
|---|---|
| 0.7 | ~63% |
| 1.3 | ~84% |
| 2.0 | ~96% |
| 5.4 | ~100% |

The OH + n-alkane series from two sessions ago sits on it (68%, 86%, 95%, 99.9% at those ratios). Your fine-structure datum sits below it, which is the anomaly above. Two unrelated observables on one curve is worth having, and it converts §15.2's fourth condition from a passing remark into an admission test computable before any prediction: min fractional step ≥ ~5× fractional 1σ.

That also collapses your exclusion list. (ii) shrinks the numerator, precision inflates the denominator, and (iii) is the degenerate case where no step exists. Only (i) is structurally different, because a node breaks monotonicity rather than resolution — and your own Sr I numbers show it, 100% away from the node and 79% across it, a failure of a different shape from 35.3%.

**4. §15.4's third question is stale.** "Whether the bracketing method transfers to non-atomic ordered systems, which we have not attempted" — it's been attempted. OH + n-alkanes, Atkinson 2003 evaluated data, C1–C13, one channel, monotone, spanning 2,359×. It fails, on precision alone, with a mechanism. Also worth stating there: 18% of lower-carbon pairs violate monotonicity if you drop the straight-chain restriction, which is Rule 1's second clause doing the same work it does for Sc III 3d, in a completely different system. That's a transfer result even though the method doesn't transfer.

**5. Abstract oversells relative to §9.** "295 of 295 interior cells" appears in the abstract without the 22-channel caveat that §9 supplies two pages later. Move it up. A referee who finds the caveat after being given the headline will trust the rest of the paper less than it deserves.

**6. §11.2's Ba I table reports one interval four times.** 6s13f through 6s16f all show [41,251, 41,648] — one measured neighbour above, so the bracket carries no cell-specific content for those four rows. It's correct, but formatted as four predictions it reads like more than it is. Either merge the rows or annotate.

**Two additions I'd make.** §15.2 becomes the admission test rather than a claim of ignorance, which makes "we know of no other observable with all four" into something searchable — and points at rotational constants and PFI-ZEKE energies, where precision is absurd and the open risk is that the same series that give you precision also asymptote. And half a subsection on measurement scheduling: on a chain, bisection is exactly optimal, so the question is empty in 1D; on Λ it isn't, adaptive scheduling beats structure-only by 2.4× at budget 48, and the algorithmic content is generic to posets of dimension ≥ 2 rather than special to Λ. The one Λ-specific fact worth the space is that Λ has no top — 5f¹⁴, 6d¹⁰, 7p⁶ are its three maximal cells — so two-sided bracketing anywhere is gated on the region where data is worst.

1	---
     2	name: file-reading
     3	description: "Use this skill when a file has been uploaded but its content is NOT in your context — only its path at /mnt/user-data/uploads/ is listed in an uploaded_files block. This skill is a router: it tells you which tool to use for each file type (pdf, docx, xlsx, csv, json, images, archives, ebooks) so you read the right amount the right way instead of blindly running cat on a binary. Triggers: any mention of /mnt/user-data/uploads/, an uploaded_files section, a file_path tag, or a user asking about an uploaded file you have not yet read. Do NOT use this skill if the file content is already visible in your context inside a documents block — you already have it."
     4	compatibility: "claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Cowork — any surface where uploads land at /mnt/user-data/uploads/"
     5	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     6	---
     7	
     8	# Reading Uploaded Files
     9	
    10	## Why this skill exists
    11	
    12	When a user uploads a file in claude.ai, Claude Desktop, or Cowork,
    13	the file is written to `/mnt/user-data/uploads/<filename>` and you are told the path
    14	in an `<uploaded_files>` block. **The content is not in your context.**
    15	You must go read it.
    16	
    17	The naive thing — `cat /mnt/user-data/uploads/whatever` — is wrong for
    18	most files:
    19	
    20	- On a PDF it prints binary garbage.
    21	- On a 100MB CSV it floods your context with rows you will never use.
    22	- On a DOCX it prints the raw ZIP bytes.
    23	- On an image it does nothing useful at all.
    24	
    25	This skill tells you the right first move for each type, and when to
    26	hand off to a deeper skill.
    27	
    28	## General protocol
    29	
    30	1. **Look at the extension.** That is your dispatch key.
    31	2. **Stat before you read.** Large files need sampling, not slurping.
    32	   ```bash
    33	   stat -c '%s bytes, %y' /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    34	   file /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    35	   ```
    36	3. **Read just enough to answer the user's question.** If they asked
    37	   "how many rows are in this CSV", don't load the whole thing into
    38	   pandas — `wc -l` gives a fast approximation (it counts newlines,
    39	   not CSV records, so it may over-count if quoted fields contain
    40	   embedded newlines).
    41	4. **If a dedicated skill exists, go read it.** The table below tells
    42	   you when. The dedicated skills cover editing, creating, and advanced
    43	   operations that this skill does not.
    44	
    45	## `extract-text`
    46	
    47	For docx, odt, epub, xlsx, pptx, rtf, and ipynb the first move is
    48	`extract-text <file>`. It emits markdown for docx/odt/epub (headings,
    49	bold, lists, links, tables), tab-separated rows under `## Sheet:`
    50	headers for xlsx, text under `## Slide N` headers for pptx, fenced
    51	code cells for ipynb, and plain text for rtf. Pass `--format <fmt>`
    52	when the extension is wrong or absent (e.g., `--format xlsx` on an
    53	`.xlsm`). If it errors on a file, `pandoc <file> -t plain` is a
    54	fallback; for xlsx/pptx, fall back to the dedicated skill's
    55	Python-based approach (openpyxl / python-pptx).
    56	
    57	## Dispatch table
    58	
    59	Where a dedicated skill is named below, invoke it by name if you have a
    60	Skill tool, or Read its SKILL.md (listed in your available skills, or in
    61	the same skills directory as this file).
    62	
    63	| Extension                         | First move                                           | Dedicated skill |
    64	| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
    65	| `.pdf`                            | Content inventory (see PDF section)                  | `pdf-reading`   |
    66	| `.docx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `docx`          |
    67	| `.doc` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.docx` first                             | `docx`          |
    68	| `.xlsx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `xlsx`          |
    69	| `.xlsm`                           | `extract-text --format xlsx`                         | `xlsx`          |
    70	| `.xls` (legacy)                   | `pd.read_excel(engine="xlrd")` — openpyxl rejects it | `xlsx`          |
    71	| `.ods`                            | `pd.read_excel(engine="odf")` — openpyxl rejects it  | `xlsx`          |
    72	| `.pptx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `pptx`          |
    73	| `.ppt` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.pptx` first                             | `pptx`          |
    74	| `.csv`, `.tsv`                    | `pandas` with `nrows`                                | — (below)       |
    75	| `.json`, `.jsonl`                 | `jq` for structure                                   | — (below)       |
    76	| `.jpg`, `.png`, `.gif`, `.webp`   | Already in your context as vision input              | — (below)       |
    77	| `.zip`, `.tar`, `.tar.gz`         | List contents, do **not** auto-extract               | — (below)       |
    78	| `.gz` (single file)               | `zcat \| head` — no manifest to list                 | — (below)       |
    79	| `.epub`, `.odt`                   | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    80	| `.rtf`                            | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    81	| `.ipynb`                          | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    82	| `.txt`, `.md`, `.log`, code files | `wc -c` then `head` or full `cat`                    | — (below)       |
    83	| Unknown                           | `file` then decide                                   | —               |
    84	
    85	---
    86	
    87	## PDF
    88	
    89	**Never** `cat` a PDF — it prints binary garbage.
    90	
    91	Quick first move — get the page count and determine whether the PDF
    92	has an extractable text layer:
    93	
    94	```bash
    95	pdfinfo /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    96	pdffonts /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    97	```
    98	
    99	`pdffonts` tells you whether text extraction will work before you try it:
   100	
   101	- **No fonts listed** (empty table, just the header) → the PDF is a
   102	  scan or raster export. `pdftotext` and `PdfReader.extract_text()`
   103	  will return nothing useful. Go straight to page rasterization or OCR
   104	  — see the `pdf-reading` skill → "Scanned documents".
   105	- **Fonts listed** → there is a text layer; extract it:
   106	  ```bash
   107	  pdftotext -f 1 -l 1 /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf - | head -20
   108	  ```
   109	
   110	The reason to check `pdffonts` first is user-facing: running
   111	`pdftotext` on a scan produces an empty result, and in a visible
   112	transcript that reads as a failed first attempt before you fall back
   113	to OCR. The two-line diagnostic above costs one tool call and avoids
   114	that — you arrive at the right method on the first try, which is what
   115	a user perceives as "it just read my file."
   116	
   117	That also shapes how to open your reply. The diagnostic commands are
   118	plumbing, not content; lead with what the user asked about. On a
   119	scanned receipt that might be "This is a 3-page scanned invoice; the
   120	amount due on page 2 is $1,845.00," and on a digitally-authored report
   121	it might be "The Q3 report runs 28 pages; revenue on p. 4 is $12.3M,
   122	up 9% YoY." What you're steering away from is the "I'll examine the
   123	PDF" / "Let me check if this is extractable" preamble — the answer to
   124	their question is the first thing they should see.
   125	
   126	For anything beyond a quick peek — figures, tables, attachments,
   127	forms, scanned PDFs, visual inspection, or choosing a reading strategy
   128	— go read the `pdf-reading` skill. It covers content inventory, text
   129	extraction vs. page rasterization, embedded content extraction, and
   130	document-type-aware reading strategies.
   131

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"# Indexing Without Prediction

## Maximality and Empirical Boundary of the Lach Elemental Lattice

---

**Status of this draft.** Prepared for independent review. Every numerical claim
below was computed during the development of this work and is reproducible from
the data sources cited in Appendix C. Section 15 lists claims made in earlier
versions of this framework that are withdrawn. Readers checking this work are
asked to attack Section 6.4 first; Conjecture 6.1 is the one place where a
result is claimed on the strength of a single failed attempt, and the authors
know it.

---

## Abstract

We construct a lattice Λ₈ over atomic electron configurations, prove it maximal
in a precise sense, and establish empirically that its order structure supplies
no predictive information beyond the coordinates from which it is built.

Λ₈ is a closed distributive lattice of order dimension exactly eight, generated
by an admissibility condition requiring every constraint to take the form
*x ≤ φ(y)* with φ non-decreasing in a single coordinate and a constant floor.
We prove that no further axis can be *derived* from the eight electronic
coordinates: a function whose graph preserves closure is forced to be monotone,
a monotone function's graph is order-isomorphic to the lattice, and the
dimension therefore cannot rise. The lattice is nonetheless
extensible by *independent* physical quantities — the parent ion's total angular
momentum, the total atomic angular momentum, the jK intermediate label, nuclear
spin — each contributing exactly one dimension. Λ₁₁ so constructed is injective
on every test case we have assembled.

Against this we set an empirical result of the opposite sign. A bracketing
method for Rydberg binding energies, derived entirely from *T = Z*²*R*/ν² and
using none of the lattice's order structure, produces containment intervals that
hold in 295 of 295 interior cells across hydrogen, four alkaline earths, three
alkali-like ions and a noble gas, spanning Z_eff = 1–3, ℓ = 0–5, single-, two-
and multi-limit systems, and both bound and autoionising regimes. Its
uncertainty estimate is derived rather than calibrated and returns ±1σ coverage
of 68.1%, 68.2% and 76.7% in the three limit regimes.

Six independent attempts to extract predictive uplift from the lattice's order —
rank aggregation, comparability, zero-shot subset selection, closure-as-existence,
join-based configuration mixing, and a derived ordinal coordinate — all failed,
each by a distinct and identifiable mechanism. We show these reduce to a single
theorem: on a product order, join, meet and comparability are definable from the
coordinates, so lattice quantities can restate the coordinates but never exceed
them. This theorem is indifferent to dimension and to how faithfully the lattice
represents the physics. Perfecting the index does not move the predictive
boundary.

The one thing that escapes the theorem is deductive containment, because a
bracket is not a function of the coordinates: it is an entailment of the order
relation given monotonicity. That is the sense in which an ordinal structure over
configuration space is useful, and the only sense we have been able to verify.

---

# Part 0 — Origin and Orientation

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 Where this began

This framework began as a three-dimensional recoding of the periodic table. Each
element was assigned a triple (*n*, ℓ, *k*): the principal quantum number of the
subshell being filled, its orbital angular momentum, and the occupancy of that
subshell. Under the componentwise partial order, the set of such triples forms a
lattice, and the periodic table becomes a path through it.

The recoding is exact and it is not new physics — it is a bijective relabelling
of information already present in the Madelung filling order. Its interest was
pedagogical and structural: the periodic table's periodicity appears as a
projection of a three-dimensional object, and elements that are chemically
analogous are close in the lattice for a structural reason rather than by
convention.

Three subsequent additions produced the object studied here. Excited
configurations required distinguishing the subshell an electron *leaves* from
the one it *enters*, giving a second triple (*e*, *f*, *g*) — target shell,
target subshell, and number of electrons transferred. Ionisation required a
count *q* of electrons removed from the source. Spin multiplicity required a
coordinate *S*. The result is Λ₈, an eight-dimensional lattice whose cells index
electron configurations relative to a reference state.

The framework's earlier claims concerned prediction: that the lattice's order,
closure and dimension would constrain atomic properties in ways the coordinates
alone did not. This paper reports that those claims are false, establishes why
in a form we believe is a theorem rather than a limitation of effort, and
reports what survives.

### 1.2 What this paper claims

**Structural (Part I).** Λ₈ is closed under join and meet, has order dimension
exactly eight, and is maximal under derivation. It extends by one dimension per
independent physical degree of freedom. As an index of atomic energy levels it
achieves 86% coverage and, at eleven dimensions, injectivity on every test case.
The physical subset of the lattice is *not* a sublattice, and no choice of
coordinates makes it one.

**Empirical (Part II).** A four-rule bracketing method for Rydberg binding
energies, each rule derived from the definition *T = Z*²*R*/ν², produces
deductive containment verified on 295 interior cells with no exceptions, and an
uncertainty estimate that requires no calibration. Its domain is bounded by four
exclusions, each with an identified mechanism.

**Thesis (Part III).** The lattice's order structure contributes nothing to the
method. Six independent tests establish this, and a theorem about product orders
explains why. The theorem does not depend on the lattice's dimension or on how
faithfully it represents the physics, so improving the index — which we do in
Part I — leaves the predictive boundary exactly where it was.

### 1.3 What this paper does not claim

We do not claim novel physics. Every quantitative result in Part II is a
consequence of the Rydberg formula and the quantum defect; the lattice's role is
to make "interior on some axis" and "same channel" well defined. We do not claim
the method extends to properties other than energies; Section 11 reports two
attempts and both failed, for reasons we characterise. We do not claim the
maximality result in the single-coordinate form asserted in earlier versions;
Section 4.2 gives counterexamples to it and shows why the maximality corollary
does not depend on it.

An earlier line of this work concerned applications to condensed-matter nuclear
phenomena. That material is removed entirely from this paper. It rested on
extensions of Λ₈ whose structural status we now know to be defective
(Appendix A), and revisiting it requires first resolving the multi-target
representation problem.

---

# Part I — Structure

## 2. Construction

### 2.1 The admissibility condition

Let Λ be a subset of ℕ^d defined by a family of constraints. We call the family
**admissible** — the condition previously designated §9.4 — if every constraint
has the form

> *x_i* ≤ φ(*x_j*)  with φ non-decreasing, together with a constant floor
> *x_i* ≥ *c*.

**Proposition 2.1.** *An admissible constraint family defines a set closed under
componentwise join and meet.*

*Proof.* Let *a*, *b* ∈ Λ and consider *x_i* ≤ φ(*x_j*). For the join,
max(*a_i*, *b_i*) = *a_i* or *b_i*; say *a_i*. Then *a_i* ≤ φ(*a_j*) ≤
φ(max(*a_j*, *b_j*)) since φ is non-decreasing. For the meet,
min(*a_i*, *b_i*) ≤ *a_i* ≤ φ(*a_j*), and we require ≤ φ(min(*a_j*, *b_j*)).
Let *w* be whichever of *a*, *b* has the smaller *j*-th coordinate. Then
min(*a_i*, *b_i*) ≤ *w_i* ≤ φ(*w_j*) = φ(min(*a_j*, *b_j*)). A constant floor is preserved by both
operations trivially. ∎

Two consequences shape everything that follows. A bound on a **sum** of two
coordinates is not of admissible form, and generally breaks closure — this is
what defeats the multi-target extension of Appendix A. A **varying floor** is
likewise inadmissible, and this is what places the physical selection rules
outside the language (Section 6.3).

### 2.2 The eight axes

| axis | meaning | bound | form |
|---|---|---|---|
| *n* | source shell | 1 ≤ *n* ≤ *N* | free root |
| ℓ | source subshell | ℓ ≤ *n* − 1 | non-decr. in *n* |
| *k* | source occupancy | 1 ≤ *k* ≤ 2(2ℓ+1) | non-decr. in ℓ |
| *q* | electrons removed | 0 ≤ *q* ≤ *k* | non-decr. in *k* |
| *e* | target shell | 1 ≤ *e* ≤ *E* | free root |
| *f* | target subshell | *f* ≤ *e* − 1 | non-decr. in *e* |
| *g* | electrons transferred | *g* ≤ min(*q*, 2(2*f*+1)) | min of two admissible |
| 2*S* | spin multiplicity | 0 ≤ 2*S* ≤ *k* | non-decr. in *k* |

Derived quantities include the net charge *c* = *q* − *g*, the electron count
*N* = C(*n*,ℓ) + *k* − *c*, and the target occupancy *G*. **These are derived
precisely because they cannot be coordinates**: each is a difference or sum of
two axes, hence not of admissible form. Section 4.3 makes this exact.

### 2.3 Closure and dimension

Closure follows from Proposition 2.1 and was additionally verified on 8 × 10⁶
sampled pairs at caps covering the observed data (*n* ≤ 6, ℓ ≤ 3, *e* ≤ 62,
*f* ≤ 3), with zero failures.

**Order dimension is exactly eight.** The upper bound is immediate: Λ₈ ⊆ ℕ⁸.
The lower bound follows from an explicit 8-box at

> (*n*, ℓ, *k*, *q*, *e*, *f*, *g*, 2*S*) = (3, 1, 2, 1, 2, 0, 0, 0)

all 2⁸ = 256 corners of which are admissible. The box is **cap-independent**: it
remains valid at cap settings (4,2,4,2), (6,3,8,3) and (8,4,12,4).

> **Figure 1.** The §9.4 constraint DAG. Nodes are axes; an edge *y* → *x*
> indicates *x* is bounded by φ(*y*). Two roots, *n* and *e*; the graph is a
> forest, not a chain. Reproduces the dependency structure that determines which
> axes can be independently varied.

> **Figure 2.** Projection of the 8-box onto three coordinate triples, showing
> all 256 corners present. Demonstrates dimension 8 visually.

### 2.4 A note on cell counts

Earlier versions of this framework reported |Λ₈| = 61,453 as a structural
invariant. It is not. That figure is the cell count at one particular choice of
caps (*n* ≤ 4, ℓ ≤ 2, *e* ≤ 5, *f* ≤ 2), and it changes with them. Every
quantity derived from it — the fraction of cells representing inward
transitions, the fraction "realisable" — is likewise a truncation artefact and
is withdrawn *as a property of Λ₈*. The invariants of Λ₈ are its closure, its
order dimension, and its maximality; its cardinality is not among them.

Such fractions may still be reported as measurements on a **named** enumeration,
and one is (§5.3). The rule observed hereafter is that any figure of the form
"X% of Λ₈" states its caps and claims nothing beyond them. Fractions of this
kind fall monotonically as the cap on *e* rises, because raising that cap adds
only outward cells; no limiting value should be read off them.

## 3. Algebra and geometry, axis by axis

Each axis has an *algebra* — the bound that defines it and its admissible form —
and a *geometry* — the shape of the region it occupies. This section also
reports, for each axis, where it is actually exercised, which turns out to vary
enormously.

**3.1 *n*, the source shell.** Algebra: a free root; every electronic bound
descends from it. Geometry: a chain, 1 to *N*. Exercised: distinguishes species,
but is **constant within any one atom**. In the axis-ablation study (§3.10),
removing *n* from the index of a single species costs zero collisions.

**3.2 ℓ, the source subshell.** Algebra: ℓ ≤ *n* − 1, non-decreasing in *n*.
Geometry: a right triangle in the (*n*, ℓ) plane. Exercised: distinguishes
species and blocks; constant within an atom.

**3.3 *k*, the source occupancy.** Algebra: 1 ≤ *k* ≤ 2(2ℓ+1). Geometry: a
staircase whose width doubles-and-adds-four with ℓ — 2, 6, 10, 14. Exercised:
constant within an atom. *k* is the coordinate that bounds *q*, 2*S*, and (in
Λ₉ and above) the angular momentum axes, so it is structurally central while
being empirically inert within a species.

**3.4 *q*, electrons removed.** Algebra: 0 ≤ *q* ≤ *k*, a triangle nested inside
*k*. Geometry: for each *k*, a chain of length *k*+1. Exercised: separates
neutral from ionised species. Constant (*q* = 1) across all singly-excited
states of one atom.

**3.5 *e*, the target shell.** Algebra: a second free root. Geometry: a chain.
Exercised: **this is the workhorse.** Removing *e* from the Ca I index costs 13
collisions in 27 levels; from Kr I, 22 in 46. It is the axis the bracketing

> **Figure 3.** Λ₈ decomposed: the (*n*, ℓ, *k*) source block, the

| axis | Ca I (27 levels) | Kr I (46 levels) |
|---|---|---|
| *n*, ℓ, *k*, *q*, *g* | 0 collisions | 0 collisions |
| *e* | **13** | **22** |
| *f* | **7** | **22** |
| 2*S* | **5** | undefined |
