{"returncode":0,"stdout":"## Abstract

We construct a lattice Λ₈ over atomic electron configurations, prove it maximal
in a precise sense, and establish empirically that its order structure supplies
no predictive information beyond the coordinates from which it is built.

Λ₈ is a closed distributive lattice of order dimension exactly eight, generated
by an admissibility condition requiring every constraint to take the form
*x ≤ φ(y)* with φ non-decreasing in a single coordinate and a constant floor.
We prove that no further axis can be *derived* from the eight electronic
coordinates: a function whose graph preserves closure is forced to be monotone,
a monotone function's graph is order-isomorphic to the lattice, and the
dimension therefore cannot rise. The lattice is nonetheless
extensible by *independent* physical quantities — the parent ion's total angular
momentum, the total atomic angular momentum, the jK intermediate label, nuclear
spin — each contributing exactly one dimension. Λ₁₁ so constructed is injective
on every test case we have assembled.

Against this we set an empirical result of the opposite sign. A bracketing
method for Rydberg binding energies, derived entirely from *T = Z*²*R*/ν² and
using none of the lattice's order structure, produces containment intervals that
hold in 295 of 295 interior cells across hydrogen, four alkaline earths, three
alkali-like ions and a noble gas, spanning Z_eff = 1–3, ℓ = 0–5, single-, two-
and multi-limit systems, and both bound and autoionising regimes. Its
uncertainty estimate is derived rather than calibrated and returns ±1σ coverage
of 68.1%, 68.2% and 76.7% in the three limit regimes.

Six independent attempts to extract predictive uplift from the lattice's order —
rank aggregation, comparability, zero-shot subset selection, closure-as-existence,
join-based configuration mixing, and a derived ordinal coordinate — all failed,
each by a distinct and identifiable mechanism. We show these reduce to a single
theorem: on a product order, join, meet and comparability are definable from the
coordinates, so lattice quantities can restate the coordinates but never exceed
them. This theorem is indifferent to dimension and to how faithfully the lattice
represents the physics. Perfecting the index does not move the predictive
boundary.

The one thing that escapes the theorem is deductive containment, because a
bracket is not a function of the coordinates: it is an entailment of the order
relation given monotonicity. That is the sense in which an ordinal structure over
configuration space is useful, and the only sense we have been able to verify.

All six review points implemented, plus the two additions. What changed:

**§12** now separates the information bound from the estimation claim, and says outright that a referee is entitled to try a seventh attempt. The thesis is restated as a conjunction — proved theorem plus six characterised failures — rather than as a proof of impossibility. Propagated to the abstract and §1.2.

**§13.2** now gives its mechanism as *a coordinate-based control reproduces the output*, not *it's an entailment of monotonicity*, with an explicit note that §14 turns on keeping those apart. §14 carries the matching sentence. The inconsistency is gone.

**§10** is rebuilt. Exclusion (ii) keeps its number and its data but loses "a constant is not monotone," and the 35.3% figure is now flagged as sitting fifteen points below the floor flatness permits — recorded as unresolved rather than papered over. New (v) for precision. Two new subsections: §10.1 gives the containment curve and the *r* = step/σ reduction, §10.2 gives the OH + *n*-alkane test with the C4/C7/C9/C12 table, the 18% channel-violation result, and the correlated-error caveat.

**§15.2** is now an admission test with a stated threshold rather than a claim of ignorance, and names where to look next. **§15.4** closes the transfer question, opens the 35.3% anomaly.

**Abstract** carries the 22-channel caveat and drops "restate but never exceed." **§11.2** merges the four identical Ba I rows into one, with a sentence on why.

**§14.1** is the scheduling subsection — chain control, the three-strategy table, data-dependence, and the paragraph conceding the algorithmic content is generic to dimension ≥ 2, with the no-top-element fact as the part that's yours.

Also: §15.3 gains three withdrawn claims (items 10–12), Appendix B documents the Monte Carlo and scheduling methods, Appendix C gains the Atkinson citation, Figure 11 is specified, and the status note now directs attackers to §6.4, §12 and §10.1 rather than §6.4 alone.

One thing I did not do: §10.2 asserts OH + alkanes was "the one system meeting §15.2's other three conditions that we could find." That's true of what we tested but it's a search claim, and you may want to soften it or actually run the search before submission.

The claim didn't need softening. It needed deleting, and it took a second claim with it.

**Observables passing the admission test are common.** Five of eight channels admit, three of them outside atomic physics: *n*-alkane boiling points (min *r* = 60), ΔH_vap (24), melting points from C₄ up (11), and total nuclear binding energy along the Sn isotopic chain (~1,400). §15.2's "we know of no other atomic observable with all four" was a statement about your search, not about nature. Withdrawn as item 13.

**And the test turns out to be weak, which is the more useful finding.** Passing means the bracket *holds*; it says nothing about whether the bracket is *worth reporting*. Defining *V* = bracket width over the error of two-point interpolation between the same two neighbours:

| channel | *V* |
|---|---|
| ΔH_vap | 80 |
| boiling points | 49 |
| Sn binding energy | 30 |
| OH + alkanes | 30 |
| **Ba I 6s*n*f — your case** | **19** |
| *n*-alkane melting points | **2.9** |

Everywhere but the last row, linear interpolation between the very neighbours forming the bracket is 19–80× more accurate than the bracket is wide. That's the price of the guarantee, and it's uniform across four domains. It also lands on your own flagship: Rydberg energies are where the bracket is *least* valuable, because the Ritz expansion makes them exceptionally smooth and smoothness is exactly what a point estimator eats.

**The exception names the missing condition.** Alkane melting points step 8.5, 34.4, 4.8, 33.8, 3.3, 23.8 — odd–even packing. Monotone but rough. Interpolation's smoothness assumption fails; the order hypothesis survives. So the bracket earns its keep on sequences that are monotone *and irregular*, and is decoration on sequences that are monotone and smooth. §15.2 now has validity conditions (a) and (b) plus a value condition (c), and §15.4's open question is whether shell closures, magic numbers and phase-boundary crossings systematically produce low *V*.

Bonus, free: the melting-point channel starts at C₄ because propane melts below ethane. Rule 1's channel clause catching a monotonicity break in a third unrelated system.

Two caveats to carry into submission. The thermochemical uncertainties are typical published levels rather than a single evaluation — stated in Appendix C, and it doesn't matter because every entry clears or misses threshold by one to three orders of magnitude. The Sn binding energies are computed from representative B/A values; the *r* estimate is robust to that but the row should be recomputed from the AME2020 table before it goes out.

content.title: Conflation of Ensemble-Learned Nuclear Mass Models for Enhanced Precision
content.text:
The weighted average of these corrected residuals reduces due to their partial cancellation, yielding a significant improvement in nuclear mass predictions. Our conflated model, which integrates ensemble earning and model averaging (ELMA), achieves a root mean square error of approximately 65 keV, well below the critical threshold of 100 keV, for the complete data set of Atomic Mass Evaluation (AME2020). The validity of ELMA is demonstrated through the evaluation of *Q* values for α decay, showing a marked decrease in deviations from experimental data relative to predictions from individual nuclear mass models. We have also compiled a table of nuclear mass excesses and binding energies for about 6,300 nuclei, which serves as a valuable resource for various nuclear physics applications and is publicly accessible via the ELMA web interface (https://ddnp.in).

Here, we report a comprehensive molecular dynamics simulation study on n-alkane systems carried out with n ranging between 3 (propane) and 8 (octane), examining the odd-even effect in melting point, density, intramolecular conformational ordering, translational and rotational motion. Alternation in various properties of n-alkanes (CnH2n+2) as a function of carbon content (n) is termed odd-even effect. Here, we report a comprehensive molecular dynamics simulation study on n-alkane systems carried out with n ranging between 3 (propane) and 8 (octane), examining the odd-even effect in melting point, density, intramolecular conformational ordering, translational and rotational motion. 

We observe an odd-even alternation in these properties, but with heptane (n = 7) exhibiting anomalous behavior for all except conformational ordering. Our simulations also show the presence of odd-even behavior in rotational and translational dynamics, below and above the melting point, respectively. The results highlight the role of both molecular shape and the variation in density and their interplay in the origins of the odd-even effect. content.text: In IUPAC nomenclature, however, hexane is the unbranched isomer (n-hexane); the other four isomers are named as methylated derivatives of pentane and butane. IUPAC also uses the term as the root of many compounds with a linear six-carbon backbone, such as 2-methylhexane. Hexanes are significant constituents of gasoline. They are all colorless liquids, odorless when pure, with boiling points between 50 and 70° C. (122 and 158° F.). They are widely used as cheap, relatively safe, largely unreactive, and easily evaporated non-polar solvents. n-Heptane is the straight-chain alkane with the chemical formula H3C(CH2)5CH3 or C7H16. When used as a test fuel component in anti-knock test engines, a 100% heptane fuel is the zero point of the octane rating scale (the 100 point is a 100% iso-octane). Cyclohexane is a cycloalkane with the molecular formula C6H12. Cyclohexane is mainly used for the industrial production of adipic acid and caprolactam, which are precursors to nylon.

import numpy as np

def audit(name, x, y, sigma_abs, note=""):
    """x: channel index, y: values, sigma_abs: 1-sigma absolute measurement error (scalar or array)"""
    y=np.array(y,float); x=np.array(x,float); s=np.full(len(y),sigma_abs,float) if np.isscalar(sigma_abs) else np.array(sigma_abs,float)
    mono = np.all(np.diff(y)>0) or np.all(np.diff(y)<0)
    viol = int(np.sum(np.diff(y)<=0)) if y[-1]>y[0] else int(np.sum(np.diff(y)>=0))
    rs=[]; widths=[]; interp_err=[]
    for i in range(1,len(y)-1):
        step=min(abs(y[i]-y[i-1]),abs(y[i+1]-y[i]))
        rs.append(step/s[i])
        widths.append(abs(y[i+1]-y[i-1]))
        p=np.interp(x[i],[x[i-1],x[i+1]],[y[i-1],y[i+1]])
        interp_err.append(abs(p-y[i]))
    rs=np.array(rs); widths=np.array(widths); interp_err=np.array(interp_err)
    V = widths.mean()/max(interp_err.mean(),1e-12)
    print(f"\n{name}")
    print(f"  monotone: {'yes' if mono else f'NO ({viol} reversals)'}   interior cells: {len(rs)}   range: {y.max()/y.min() if y.min()>0 else float('nan'):.3g}x")
    print(f"  r = step/sigma : min {rs.min():.3g}  median {np.median(rs):.3g}  -> admission (>=5): {'PASS' if rs.min()>=5 else 'FAIL at some cells' if rs.max()>=5 else 'FAIL'}")
    print(f"  mean bracket width {widths.mean():.4g}   mean interp error {interp_err.mean():.4g}   V = width/err = {V:.3g}")
    if note: print(f"  {note}")
    return rs,V

    """x: channel index, y: values, sigma_abs: 1-sigma absolute measurement error (scalar or array)"""
    y=np.array(y,float); x=np.array(x,float); s=np.full(len(y),sigma_abs,float) if np.isscalar(sigma_abs) else np.array(sigma_abs,float)
    mono = np.all(np.diff(y)>0) or np.all(np.diff(y)<0)
    viol = int(np.sum(np.diff(y)<=0)) if y[-1]>y[0] else int(np.sum(np.diff(y)>=0))
    rs=[]; widths=[]; interp_err=[]
    for i in range(1,len(y)-1):
        step=min(abs(y[i]-y[i-1]),abs(y[i+1]-y[i]))
        rs.append(step/s[i])

rate coefficients with the *n*-alkanes, C₁–C₁₃, at 298 K, from the Atkinson
(2003) evaluation."""

coefficients with the *n*-alkanes, C₁–C₁₃, at 298 K, from the Atkinson (2003)
evaluation."""

old="""**The method does not transfer to chemical kinetics, and the reason is
quantitative rather than categorical.** This closes the third question of §15.4
as posed in earlier versions."""
new="""**The method does not transfer to chemical kinetics, and the reason is
quantitative rather than categorical.** This closes the third question of §15.4
as posed in earlier versions.

### 10.3 The admission test is weak, and a second condition is needed

Having a test, we applied it rather than continuing to assert scarcity. The
results below use handbook values for the thermochemical series with
uncertainties assumed at typical published levels (±0.3 K for transition
temperatures, ±0.2 kJ mol⁻¹ for evaluated enthalpies) and AME2020-scale
uncertainties for the nuclear case. The assumption does not matter: every entry
clears or misses the threshold by one to three orders of magnitude.

| channel | monotone | min *r* | admits? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rydberg *T*, Ba I 6s*n*f | yes | ~4 × 10⁵ | yes |
| Total nuclear binding energy, Sn isotopic chain | yes | ~1.4 × 10³ | yes |
| *n*-alkane boiling points, C₄–C₁₄ | yes | 60 | yes |
| *n*-alkane Δ*H*_vap(298), C₅–C₁₂ | yes | 24 | yes |
| *n*-alkane melting points, C₄–C₁₄ | yes | 11 | yes |
| *n*-alkane melting points, C₁–C₆ | **no** | 1.0 | no |
| OH + *n*-alkane rate coefficients, C₉–C₁₃ | yes | 0.7 | no |
| Fine-structure splittings, ν³-reduced | — | < 1 | no |

**Observables satisfying §15.2 are common, not rare.** Four channels in three
domains outside atomic spectroscopy admit, two of them by more than a factor of
ten above threshold. Earlier versions of this paper claimed to know of no other
observable meeting the conditions; that claim was a statement about our search,
not about nature, and it is withdrawn (§15.3). The correct generalisation is not
*energies* but *any quantity measured far better than it varies between adjacent
cells*, which is a property of measurement technique as much as of physics.

**This makes the admission test necessary and clearly not sufficient.** Passing
it means the bracket holds. It says nothing about whether the bracket is worth
reporting. Define

> *V* = (mean bracket width) / (mean error of linear interpolation between the
> same two neighbours),

the factor by which the guarantee costs precision. Across every admitted channel
we tested:

| channel | mean bracket width | interp. error | *V* |
|---|---|---|---|
| *n*-alkane Δ*H*_vap | 10.0 kJ mol⁻¹ | 0.13 | **80** |
| *n*-alkane boiling points | 50.4 K | 1.02 | **49** |
| Sn binding energy | 15.9 MeV | 0.54 | **30** |
| OH + alkane kinetics | 95% of value | 3.2% | **30** |
| Ba I 6s*n*f (this paper's own case) | 397 cm⁻¹ | 20.5 cm⁻¹ | **19** |
| ***n*-alkane melting points** | **29.8 K** | **10.3 K** | **2.9** |

Everywhere but the last row, a two-point linear interpolation between the very
neighbours that form the bracket is twenty to eighty times more accurate than the
bracket is wide. §14 argues that the bracket buys guarantee rather than
precision; this is the price of the guarantee, and it is uniform across domains.
It also bears on this paper's own flagship result: **Rydberg energies are the
case where the bracket is least valuable**, because the Ritz expansion makes them
exceptionally smooth, and smoothness is exactly what a point estimator exploits.

The exception identifies the missing condition. Melting points of the
*n*-alkanes alternate — successive steps of 8.5, 34.4, 4.8, 33.8, 3.3, 23.8,
4.1, 16.0, 4.2, 11.2 K, the odd–even packing effect — so the sequence is
monotone but not smooth. Interpolation's smoothness assumption fails; the order
hypothesis does not. **The bracket earns its keep on sequences that are monotone
and irregular, and is decoration on sequences that are monotone and smooth.**
The channel also begins at C₄ rather than C₁, because propane melts below ethane
— a monotonicity break that Rule 1's channel clause catches, in a third
independent system.

We state this as the sharper form of the paper's thesis. An order supplies
containment; containment is worth having when interpolation is untrustworthy;
and interpolation is untrustworthy exactly where the sequence is rough. That is a
narrower and more defensible claim than the one Part II was originally built to
support."""
assert s.count(old)==1; s=s.replace(old,new)
open(p,'w').write(s); print("10.2/10.3 done")

# --- 15.2: two-condition admission test ---
old="""> **Admit an observable to the method iff** (a) it is monotone in the order with
> no sign change on the channel, and (b) the minimum fractional step between
> adjacent measured cells in that channel is at least ~5× the fractional 1σ
> measurement error.

Condition (b) is checkable from a data table alone and costs nothing. Applied
retrospectively it admits Rydberg energies by five orders of magnitude, rejects
fine-structure splittings, rejects OH + alkane kinetics at C ≥ 9, and rejects
Ti I for want of any step at all.

We no longer claim to know of no other observable meeting the conditions; we
claim only not to have searched systematically. The test above makes such a
search cheap, and the place we would look is where precision is extreme and
spacing coarse — rotational constants, PFI-ZEKE ionisation energies,
vibrational fundamentals in isotopologue series. The risk we would expect there
is that the same homologous structure supplying interior cells also drives the
observable toward an asymptote, trading condition (b)'s denominator against its
numerator along the same axis. Characterising that trade is the natural next
experiment and we have not done it."""
new="""> **Validity.** The bracket holds iff (a) the observable is monotone in the order
> with no sign change on the channel, and (b) the minimum fractional step between
> adjacent measured cells is at least ~5× the fractional 1σ measurement error.
>
> **Value.** The bracket is worth reporting iff, in addition, (c) the sequence is
> not smooth in the channel index — quantified by *V* of §10.3, the ratio of
> bracket width to the error of two-point interpolation between the same
> neighbours. Small *V* means the order is contributing; large *V* means a point
> estimator has already done the work.

Both are checkable from a data table alone. Applied to eight channels in §10.3,
(a) and (b) admit five, including three outside atomic physics, so **observables
meeting the original four conditions are common rather than rare** and the
scarcity claimed in earlier versions is withdrawn (§15.3). Condition (c) is the
binding one: of the five admitted channels, four have *V* between 19 and 80, and
only *n*-alkane melting points — monotone but alternating, hence rough — return
*V* ≈ 3.

This reverses the emphasis of the earlier account. Energies were never special
for being energies; they are special for being measured to 10⁻³ cm⁻¹ against
spacings of hundreds of wavenumbers, which is a fact about spectroscopy. And the
smoothness that makes the Ritz expansion work is the same smoothness that makes
the bracket redundant, so Part II's own domain is where the order contributes
least. The place to look for cases where it contributes most is not where
precision is highest but where **monotone physics produces irregular sequences** —
odd–even effects, shell closures, packing transitions, and other structural
alternations. We have not searched systematically for those, and it is the search
we would now run first."""
assert s.count(old)==1; s=s.replace(old,new)

# --- 15.3: withdraw the scarcity claim ---
old="""12. **Four independent exclusions.** Three of the five in §10 are one ratio at
    different values (§10.1)."""
new="""12. **Four independent exclusions.** Three of the five in §10 are one ratio at
    different values (§10.1).
13. **"We know of no other atomic observable with all four properties."** A
    statement about our search rather than about nature, and false. Applying the
    admission test to eight channels admits five, three of them outside atomic
    physics (§10.3). What is scarce is not observables that satisfy the
    conditions but observables for which the resulting bracket beats a two-point
    interpolation, and the paper previously had no condition distinguishing the
    two."""
assert s.count(old)==1; s=s.replace(old,new)

# --- 15.4 open questions ---
old="""**Whether any observable passes the admission test of §15.2.** Now a search
rather than a claim of ignorance, and the candidates are named there."""
new="""**Where condition (c) of §15.2 is satisfied.** Many observables pass validity;
almost none of those tested pass value. The one that does is rough for a
structural reason — odd–even chain packing. Whether shell closures, magic
numbers, phase-boundary crossings and similar structural alternations
systematically produce low *V* is open, and it is the question that determines
whether the method has a domain of its own or is a consistency check on
interpolation."""

construction, and the failure rate of the fitted interval is precisely what the

bracket does not have. The guarantee is not free: §10.3 measures its price at a
factor of 19 to 80 in width against two-point interpolation across five domains,
including this paper's own Rydberg case at 19."""

> bracket width to the error of two-point interpolation between the same

> estimator has already done the work.

The claim didn't need softening. It needed deleting, and it took a second claim with it.

**Observables passing the admission test are common.** Five of eight channels admit, three of them outside atomic physics: *n*-alkane boiling points (min *r* = 60), ΔH_vap (24), melting points from C₄ up (11), and total nuclear binding energy along the Sn isotopic chain (~1,400). §15.2's "we know of no other atomic observable with all four" was a statement about your search, not about nature. Withdrawn as item 13.

**And the test turns out to be weak, which is the more useful finding.** Passing means the bracket *holds*; it says nothing about whether the bracket is *worth reporting*. Defining *V* = bracket width over the error of two-point interpolation between the same two neighbours:

| channel | *V* |
|---|---|
| ΔH_vap | 80 |
| boiling points | 49 |
| Sn binding energy | 30 |
| OH + alkanes | 30 |
| **Ba I 6s*n*f — your case** | **19** |
| *n*-alkane melting points | **2.9** |

Everywhere but the last row, linear interpolation between the very neighbours forming the bracket is 19–80× more accurate than the bracket is wide. That's the price of the guarantee, and it's uniform across four domains. It also lands on your own flagship: Rydberg energies are where the bracket is *least* valuable, because the Ritz expansion makes them exceptionally smooth and smoothness is exactly what a point estimator eats.

**The exception names the missing condition.** Alkane melting points step 8.5, 34.4, 4.8, 33.8, 3.3, 23.8 — odd–even packing. Monotone but rough. Interpolation's smoothness assumption fails; the order hypothesis survives. So the bracket earns its keep on sequences that are monotone *and irregular*, and is decoration on sequences that are monotone and smooth. §15.2 now has validity conditions (a) and (b) plus a value condition (c), and §15.4's open question is whether shell closures, magic numbers and phase-boundary crossings systematically produce low *V*.

Bonus, free: the melting-point channel starts at C₄ because propane melts below ethane. Rule 1's channel clause catching a monotonicity break in a third unrelated system.

Two caveats to carry into submission. The thermochemical uncertainties are typical published levels rather than a single evaluation — stated in Appendix C, and it doesn't matter because every entry clears or misses threshold by one to three orders of magnitude. The Sn binding energies are computed from representative B/A values; the *r* estimate is robust to that but the row should be recomputed from the AME2020 table before it goes out.

**Substitution first.** The AME2020 table fetch truncated at A ≈ 84, short of Sn at A = 112–124. It did return the complete Ni chain, so I used Z = 28, A = 56–73, experimental values only, taking binding energy per nucleon and its published 1σ directly from the file rather than reconstructing from mass excesses. Sixteen interior cells, σ from 0.35 to 3.73 keV on totals of 484–617 MeV. If you want Sn specifically it's the same calculation on a different block of the same table.

**What changed.** Min *r* = 1.2 × 10³, essentially as estimated. But *V* came out at **10.9, not 30** — the bracket is nearly three times more useful than I claimed. My estimate used a smooth B/A model, which washed out exactly the structure that matters.

**What it washed out is pairing.** One-neutron separation energies along the chain alternate: 9.35 MeV mean at odd *N* against 6.51 MeV at even *N*. The sequence is monotone and not smooth, which is precisely the condition §15.2(c) now requires — so linear interpolation carries a 1.46 MeV mean error against a 15.8 MeV bracket, an order of magnitude better ratio than the smooth channels.

|---|---|---|
| ΔH_vap, boiling points, OH kinetics | 30–80 | smooth |

cd /home/claude/survey && cat > nuclear.py << 'EOF'
import numpy as np
# AME2020 (Wang et al. 2021), BINDING ENERGY/A in keV with 1-sigma, read from mass_1.mas20
# Ni chain (Z=28), experimental values only (no '#' estimates)
rows=[(56,8642.7811,0.0071),(57,8670.9364,0.0099),(58,8732.0621,0.0060),(59,8736.5912,0.0060),
      (60,8780.7769,0.0059),(61,8765.0281,0.0058),(62,8794.5555,0.0069),(63,8763.4955,0.0068),
      (64,8777.4637,0.0072),(65,8736.2424,0.0074),(66,8739.5086,0.0212),(67,8695.7505,0.0431),
      (68,8682.4667,0.0438),(69,8623.0998,0.0540),(70,8604.2917,0.0306),(71,8543.1564,0.0315),
      (72,8520.2118,0.0311),(73,8457.6529,0.0332)]
A=np.array([r[0] for r in rows],float)
B=np.array([r[0]*r[1] for r in rows])          # total binding energy, keV
sB=np.array([r[0]*r[2] for r in rows])         # 1-sigma on total, keV

print("Ni isotopic chain, AME2020 — total binding energy")
print(f"  monotone increasing: {np.all(np.diff(B)>0)}   n = {len(A)}   interior cells = {len(A)-2}")
print(f"  B spans {B[0]/1e3:.1f} -> {B[-1]/1e3:.1f} MeV;  sigma {sB.min():.2f}-{sB.max():.2f} keV")
Sn=np.diff(B)
print(f"  one-neutron separation energies S_n (MeV): "+" ".join(f"{v/1000:.2f}" for v in Sn))
print(f"  odd-even staggering: even-N mean {np.mean(Sn[0::2])/1000:.2f}  odd-N mean {np.mean(Sn[1::2])/1000:.2f} MeV")

r=[];w=[];e=[]
for i in range(1,len(A)-1):
    step=min(abs(B[i]-B[i-1]),abs(B[i+1]-B[i]))
    r.append(step/sB[i]); w.append(abs(B[i+1]-B[i-1]))
    e.append(abs(np.interp(A[i],[A[i-1],A[i+1]],[B[i-1],B[i+1]])-B[i]))
r=np.array(r);w=np.array(w);e=np.array(e)
print(f"\n  r = step/sigma : min {r.min():.3g}  median {np.median(r):.3g}   admission (>=5): {'PASS' if r.min()>=5 else 'FAIL'}")
print(f"  mean bracket width {w.mean()/1000:.2f} MeV   mean interp error {e.mean()/1000:.3f} MeV")
print(f"  V = width/interp error = {w.mean()/e.mean():.2f}")
print(f"\n  per-cell V: "+" ".join(f"{a:.0f}:{ww/ee:.1f}" for a,ww,ee in zip(A[1:-1],w,e)))
EOF
python3 nuclear.py

input.command:
cd /home/claude/paper && python3 - << 'PYEOF'
p='v3.md'; s=open(p).read()

old="""| Total nuclear binding energy, Sn isotopic chain | yes | ~1.4 × 10³ | yes |"""
new="""| Total nuclear binding energy, Ni chain, *A* = 56–73 | yes | 1.2 × 10³ | yes |"""
assert s.count(old)==1; s=s.replace(old,new)

old="""| channel | mean bracket width | interp. error | *V* |
|---|---|---|---|
| *n*-alkane Δ*H*_vap | 10.0 kJ mol⁻¹ | 0.13 | **80** |
| *n*-alkane boiling points | 50.4 K | 1.02 | **49** |
| Sn binding energy | 15.9 MeV | 0.54 | **30** |
| OH + alkane kinetics | 95% of value | 3.2% | **30** |
| Ba I 6s*n*f (this paper's own case) | 397 cm⁻¹ | 20.5 cm⁻¹ | **19** |
| ***n*-alkane melting points** | **29.8 K** | **10.3 K** | **2.9** |

Everywhere but the last row, a two-point linear interpolation between the very
neighbours that form the bracket is twenty to eighty times more accurate than the
bracket is wide. §14 argues that the bracket buys guarantee rather than
precision; this is the price of the guarantee, and it is uniform across domains.
It also bears on this paper's own flagship result: **Rydberg energies are the
case where the bracket is least valuable**, because the Ritz expansion makes them
exceptionally smooth, and smoothness is exactly what a point estimator exploits.

The exception identifies the missing condition. Melting points of the
*n*-alkanes alternate — successive steps of 8.5, 34.4, 4.8, 33.8, 3.3, 23.8,
4.1, 16.0, 4.2, 11.2 K, the odd–even packing effect — so the sequence is
monotone but not smooth. Interpolation's smoothness assumption fails; the order
hypothesis does not. **The bracket earns its keep on sequences that are monotone
and irregular, and is decoration on sequences that are monotone and smooth.**
The channel also begins at C₄ rather than C₁, because propane melts below ethane
— a monotonicity break that Rule 1's channel clause catches, in a third
independent system."""
new="""| channel | mean bracket width | interp. error | *V* |
|---|---|---|---|
| *n*-alkane Δ*H*_vap | 10.0 kJ mol⁻¹ | 0.13 | **80** |
| *n*-alkane boiling points | 50.4 K | 1.02 | **49** |
| OH + alkane kinetics | 95% of value | 3.2% | **30** |
| Ba I 6s*n*f (this paper's own case) | 397 cm⁻¹ | 20.5 cm⁻¹ | **19** |
| **Ni binding energy, *A* = 56–73** | **15.8 MeV** | **1.46 MeV** | **10.9** |
| ***n*-alkane melting points** | **29.8 K** | **10.3 K** | **2.9** |

For the top four, a two-point linear interpolation between the very neighbours
that form the bracket is nineteen to eighty times more accurate than the bracket
is wide. §14 argues that the bracket buys guarantee rather than precision; this
is the price of the guarantee. It also bears on this paper's own flagship result:
**Rydberg energies are near the case where the bracket is least valuable**,
because the Ritz expansion makes them exceptionally smooth, and smoothness is
exactly what a point estimator exploits.

**The bottom two rows have the same cause, in unrelated physics.** Melting points
of the *n*-alkanes step by 8.5, 34.4, 4.8, 33.8, 3.3, 23.8, 4.1, 16.0, 4.2,
11.2 K — the odd–even packing effect. One-neutron separation energies along the
Ni chain alternate between a 9.35 MeV mean at odd *N* and 6.51 MeV at even *N* —
nucleon pairing. Both sequences are monotone and neither is smooth, and both
return *V* an order of magnitude below the smooth cases. **The bracket earns its
keep on sequences that are monotone and irregular, and is decoration on sequences
that are monotone and smooth**; odd–even staggering is the clearest generator of
the first kind, and it appears here in a chemical and a nuclear system with no
common mechanism beyond the alternation itself.

The alkane channel also begins at C₄ rather than C₁, because propane melts below
ethane — a monotonicity break that Rule 1's channel clause catches, in a third
independent system."""
assert s.count(old)==1; s=s.replace(old,new)

old="""and AME2020-scale uncertainties for the nuclear case. The assumption does not matter: every entry
clears or misses the threshold by one to three orders of magnitude."""
new="""for the thermochemical series. The nuclear entry uses AME2020 binding energies
per nucleon and their published 1σ uncertainties directly, with no assumption.
The thermochemical assumption does not matter: every entry clears or misses the
threshold by one to three orders of magnitude."""
assert s.count(old)==1; s=s.replace(old,new)

old="""**Where condition (c) of §15.2 is satisfied.** Many observables pass validity;
almost none of those tested pass value. The one that does is rough for a
structural reason — odd–even chain packing. Whether shell closures, magic
numbers, phase-boundary crossings and similar structural alternations
systematically produce low *V* is open, and it is the question that determines
whether the method has a domain of its own or is a consistency check on
interpolation."""
new="""**Where condition (c) of §15.2 is satisfied.** Many observables pass validity;
few pass value. The two that come closest are rough for the same formal reason in
unrelated physics — odd–even alternation, from chain packing in one case and
nucleon pairing in the other. Whether alternation is the general generator of low
*V*, and whether shell closures, magic numbers and phase-boundary crossings
behave likewise, is open. It is the question that determines whether the method
has a domain of its own or is a consistency check on interpolation, and the
nuclear chart is where we would test it: pairing is universal there, chains are
long, and AME2020 supplies uncertainties for every cell."""
assert s.count(old)==1; s=s.replace(old,new)

old="""| Wang *et al.*, *Chin. Phys. C* **45**, 030003 (2021) — AME2020 | Sn isotopic binding energies and their uncertainties (§10.3) |"""
new="""| Wang *et al.*, *Chin. Phys. C* **45**, 030003 (2021) — AME2020 | Ni binding energies per nucleon and 1σ uncertainties, *A* = 56–73, experimental values only (§10.3) |"""
assert s.count(old)==1; s=s.replace(old,new)

open(p,'w').write(s); print("ok")
PYEOF

Recomputed, and the estimate was wrong in the direction that matters.

**Substitution first.** The AME2020 table fetch truncated at A ≈ 84, short of Sn at A = 112–124. It did return the complete Ni chain, so I used Z = 28, A = 56–73, experimental values only, taking binding energy per nucleon and its published 1σ directly from the file rather than reconstructing from mass excesses. Sixteen interior cells, σ from 0.35 to 3.73 keV on totals of 484–617 MeV. If you want Sn specifically it's the same calculation on a different block of the same table.

**What changed.** Min *r* = 1.2 × 10³, essentially as estimated. But *V* came out at **10.9, not 30** — the bracket is nearly three times more useful than I claimed. My estimate used a smooth B/A model, which washed out exactly the structure that matters.

**What it washed out is pairing.** One-neutron separation energies along the chain alternate: 9.35 MeV mean at odd *N* against 6.51 MeV at even *N*. The sequence is monotone and not smooth, which is precisely the condition §15.2(c) now requires — so linear interpolation carries a 1.46 MeV mean error against a 15.8 MeV bracket, an order of magnitude better ratio than the smooth channels.

That gives the new condition a second instance, in physics unrelated to the first:

| channel | *V* | why |
|---|---|---|
| ΔH_vap, boiling points, OH kinetics | 30–80 | smooth |
| Ba I 6s*n*f | 19 | smooth (Ritz) |
| **Ni binding energy** | **10.9** | **nucleon pairing** |
| ***n*-alkane melting points** | **2.9** | **odd–even packing** |

Two systems with no common mechanism beyond the alternation itself, both landing an order of magnitude below the smooth cases. §10.3 now says that outright, and §15.4 names the nuclear chart as where to test it — pairing is universal there, chains run to twenty-plus members, and AME2020 gives an uncertainty for every cell. That's a better next experiment than the spectroscopic one I suggested two turns ago, and it's a case where the method might have a domain rather than a consistency check.

Appendix C now cites the specific quantity and the experimental-only restriction.

The survey turned up a theorem before it turned up any data, and the theorem is the result.

**Proposition 14.1.** For three consecutive cells at equal index spacing, bracket width is *d*₀+*d*₁ and two-point interpolation error is |*d*₀−*d*₁|/2, so *V* = 2(*d*₀+*d*₁)/|*d*₀−*d*₁|. Monotonicity makes both steps positive, hence |*d*₀−*d*₁| < *d*₀+*d*₁, hence **V > 2 always**, approaching 2 only as one step vanishes. Every empirical *V* in the paper — 2.9, 10.9, 19, 30, 49, 80 — is an instance of this bound, not an independent measurement. The bracket can never beat interpolation on width, for any observable, with any data. Its entire contribution is the guarantee.

**The survey then locates where the bound is tightest.** Nine even-*Z* chains, *Z* = 20–36, AME2020 experimental values only, 160 interior cells. All nine chains return *V* between 10.2 and 12.5 — and that number is predicted with no free parameter: if separation energies alternate as S̄ₙ ± Δ, then *V* = 2S̄ₙ/Δ exactly, which reproduces the measured column to within 30% across all nine. Nuclear *V* ≈ 11 *is* the ratio of separation energy to pairing gap.

**And it falls toward the drip line.** Median *V* by neutron excess: 13.24 → 11.31 → 9.95 → 8.52 → 7.90 from *N*−*Z* ≈ 0 to +20. corr(log *V*, *N*−*Z*) = −0.62, corr(log *V*, log Sₙ) = +0.69. Mechanism is the proposition read forwards — as Sₙ falls toward Δ the smaller step vanishes and alternation maximises.

**The trade you'd expect doesn't materialise.** I'd warned that whatever supplies interior cells might also flatten the observable. Here corr(log *V*, log *r*) = +0.14, and median *r* stays above 1,700 — 350× the admission threshold — even in the most neutron-rich bin. Of 24 cells with *V* < 8, all 24 also have *r* > 5. Zero useful-but-invalid. Binding energies are large and mass spectrometry is good, so precision survives far from stability while smoothness does not.

Ceiling, stated plainly in §10.4: the best single cell anywhere in any domain surveyed is ⁵⁴Ca at *V* = 4.74 against a floor of 2. The nuclear chart isn't where the order wins — Proposition 14.1 forbids that — it's a large, well-measured, physically motivated region where the guarantee is cheapest and the alternatives are extrapolating.

§15.4's open question is now sharper and experimental: reaching the floor requires Sₙ → Δ, which means the drip line, so whether measured masses ever get there with *r* still above threshold is a question about the next decade of mass spectrometry.

import numpy as np
# bracket width  w_i = |y_{i+1} - y_{i-1}|          = |d_i + d_{i-1}|   with d_i = y_{i+1}-y_i
# interp error   e_i = |y_i - (y_{i-1}+y_{i+1})/2| = |d_i - d_{i-1}|/2
# so V_i = w_i/e_i = 2|d_i+d_{i-1}| / |d_i-d_{i-1}|
# If the sequence is MONOTONE, all d>0, so |d_i-d_{i-1}| < d_i+d_{i-1} = |d_i+d_{i-1}|  =>  V_i > 2.
rng=np.random.default_rng(0); worst=1e9
for t in range(400000):
    d=rng.random(2)*rng.choice([1,1e-3,1e3])+1e-12      # two positive steps, wild ratios
    V=2*abs(d[0]+d[1])/max(abs(d[0]-d[1]),1e-300)
    worst=min(worst,V)
print('minimum V over 400k random monotone triples:', round(worst,6))
print('analytic floor: V -> 2 as one step -> 0; V -> inf as steps equalise')
for ratio in [1,1.2,2,5,20,100,1e6]:
    print(f'  step ratio {ratio:>8g} : V = {2*(1+ratio)/abs(ratio-1) if ratio!=1 else float(\"inf\"):.3f}')
"

p='v3.md'; s=open(p).read()
def rep(o,n):
    assert s.count(o)==1, f"MISS {o[:50]!r}"
    return s.replace(o,n)

# --- Proposition in section 14 ---
s=rep("""none — a regression can be made to output an interval, but not one that holds by
construction, and the failure rate of the fitted interval is precisely what the
bracket does not have. The guarantee is not free: §10.3 measures its price at a
factor of 19 to 80 in width against two-point interpolation across five domains,
including this paper's own Rydberg case at 19.""",
"""none — a regression can be made to output an interval, but not one that holds by
construction, and the failure rate of the fitted interval is precisely what the
bracket does not have.

The guarantee is not free, and its price has a floor.

> **Proposition 14.1.** *Let three consecutive cells of a channel carry values
> y₀ < y₁ < y₂ at equally spaced index. Let w = y₂ − y₀ be the deductive bracket
> width at the middle cell and e = |y₁ − (y₀+y₂)/2| the error of two-point linear
> interpolation from the same neighbours. Then V = w/e > 2, with V → 2 only as
> one of the two steps vanishes.*
>
> *Proof.* Write d₀ = y₁ − y₀ and d₁ = y₂ − y₁, both positive by monotonicity.
> Then w = d₀ + d₁ and e = |d₀ − d₁|/2, so V = 2(d₀+d₁)/|d₀−d₁|. Since d₀, d₁ > 0
> we have |d₀ − d₁| < d₀ + d₁, giving V > 2. As min(d₀,d₁)/max(d₀,d₁) → 0 the
> ratio → 2; as d₀ → d₁ it diverges. ∎

**The bracket can never be competitive with interpolation on width.** Not for
some observables, not with better data: for any monotone sequence whatever, the
deductive interval is more than twice the error of the crudest possible point
estimate built from the same two numbers. Every empirical *V* reported in §10.3
and §10.4 is an instance of this bound rather than an independent fact, and the
bound is tight only in the limit of maximal alternation. Against a better
estimator — the Ritz expansion of §8, or a nuclear mass model — the gap is wider
still, so *V* as defined understates it.

This settles what the order contributes and what it does not. It contributes
containment, which no point estimator supplies at any width. It cannot contribute
precision, and the failure is structural rather than a limitation of the data.""")

# --- new 10.4 ---
s=rep("""We state this as the sharper form of the paper's thesis. An order supplies
containment; containment is worth having when interpolation is untrustworthy;
and interpolation is untrustworthy exactly where the sequence is rough. That is a
narrower and more defensible claim than the one Part II was originally built to
support.""",
"""We state this as the sharper form of the paper's thesis. An order supplies
containment; containment is worth having when interpolation is untrustworthy;
and interpolation is untrustworthy exactly where the sequence is rough. That is a
narrower and more defensible claim than the one Part II was originally built to
support.

### 10.4 Where alternation lives: a survey of the nuclear chart

If odd–even alternation is the generator of low *V*, the nuclear chart is the
place to test it, because pairing is universal there, chains are long, and
AME2020 supplies an uncertainty for every cell. We took nine even-*Z* isotopic
chains, *Z* = 20 to 36, experimental values only: 160 interior cells.

**Every chain admits, and every chain returns the same *V*.**

| chain | *Z* | *A* range | cells | min *r* | *V* | 2S̄ₙ/Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ca | 20 | 36–56 | 19 | 10 | 11.87 | 16.1 |
| Ti | 22 | 40–58 | 17 | 15 | 11.69 | 15.3 |
| Cr | 24 | 44–64 | 19 | 47 | 11.41 | 14.1 |
| Fe | 26 | 48–67 | 18 | 612 | 12.35 | 12.9 |
| Ni | 28 | 52–73 | 20 | 602 | 12.17 | 12.8 |
| Zn | 30 | 58–82 | 23 | 521 | 10.42 | 12.4 |
| Ge | 32 | 64–83 | 18 | 154 | 10.25 | 10.2 |
| Se | 34 | 67–83 | 15 | 1136 | 10.88 | 9.9 |
| Kr | 36 | 71–83 | 11 | 1241 | 12.45 | 11.2 |

The last column is the prediction from pairing alone. If successive separation
energies alternate as S̄ₙ ± Δ, the two steps of Proposition 14.1 are d₀ = S̄ₙ+Δ
and d₁ = S̄ₙ−Δ, giving *V* = 2S̄ₙ/Δ exactly. It reproduces the measured column to
within 30% across all nine chains with no fitted parameter. **The characteristic
*V* ≈ 11 of nuclear binding energies is the ratio of the mean separation energy
to the pairing gap, and nothing else.**

**And *V* falls systematically toward the neutron drip line.** Pooling all 160
cells and binning by neutron excess:

| *N* − *Z* | cells | median *V* | median *r* | median Sₙ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| −2 to +4 | 46 | 13.24 | 1.4 × 10⁴ | 10.24 MeV |
| +4 to +8 | 36 | 11.31 | 1.8 × 10⁴ | 7.73 |
| +8 to +12 | 35 | 9.95 | 8.2 × 10³ | 5.81 |
| +12 to +16 | 28 | 8.52 | 1.8 × 10³ | 4.32 |
| +16 to +22 | 10 | 7.90 | 1.9 × 10³ | 4.02 |

corr(log *V*, *N*−*Z*) = −0.62; corr(log *V*, log Sₙ) = +0.69. The mechanism is
Proposition 14.1 read forwards: as Sₙ falls toward Δ the smaller step vanishes,
alternation becomes maximal, and *V* approaches its floor. **The bracket is at its
most useful exactly at the neutron-rich frontier**, which is where masses are
least well predicted by models and where the next generation of measurements is
aimed.

**The trade we expected does not appear.** For spectroscopy we anticipated that
the structure supplying interior cells would also drive the observable toward an
asymptote, trading condition (b) against condition (c) along one axis. Here it
does not: corr(log *V*, log *r*) = +0.14, and median *r* remains above 1,700 —
some 350 times the admission threshold — even in the most neutron-rich bin. Of
the 24 cells with *V* < 8, **all 24 also have *r* > 5, and none is useful but
invalid.** Binding energies are large and mass spectrometry is good, so precision
survives far from stability while smoothness does not.

**The honest ceiling.** The lowest single cell in the survey is ⁵⁴Ca at
*V* = 4.74, against Proposition 14.1's floor of 2. So even in the best regime we
have found, in any domain, the deductive bracket remains roughly five times wider
than a two-line interpolation between the same neighbours. What the nuclear chart
supplies is not a place where the order wins on width — Proposition 14.1 forbids
that — but a large, well-measured, physically motivated region where the cost of
the guarantee is at its lowest, and where the guarantee is worth paying for
because the alternative estimators are extrapolating.""")

content.text:
The survey turned up a theorem before it turned up any data, and the theorem is the result.

**Proposition 14.1.** For three consecutive cells at equal index spacing, bracket width is *d*₀+*d*₁ and two-point interpolation error is |*d*₀−*d*₁|/2, so *V* = 2(*d*₀+*d*₁)/|*d*₀−*d*₁|. Monotonicity makes both steps positive, hence |*d*₀−*d*₁| < *d*₀+*d*₁, hence **V > 2 always**, approaching 2 only as one step vanishes. Every empirical *V* in the paper — 2.9, 10.9, 19, 30, 49, 80 — is an instance of this bound, not an independent measurement. The bracket can never beat interpolation on width, for any observable, with any data. Its entire contribution is the guarantee.

**The survey then locates where the bound is tightest.** Nine even-*Z* chains, *Z* = 20–36, AME2020 experimental values only, 160 interior cells. All nine chains return *V* between 10.2 and 12.5 — and that number is predicted with no free parameter: if separation energies alternate as S̄ₙ ± Δ, then *V* = 2S̄ₙ/Δ exactly, which reproduces the measured column to within 30% across all nine. Nuclear *V* ≈ 11 *is* the ratio of separation energy to pairing gap.

**And it falls toward the drip line.** Median *V* by neutron excess: 13.24 → 11.31 → 9.95 → 8.52 → 7.90 from *N*−*Z* ≈ 0 to +20. corr(log *V*, *N*−*Z*) = −0.62, corr(log *V*, log Sₙ) = +0.69. Mechanism is the proposition read forwards — as Sₙ falls toward Δ the smaller step vanishes and alternation maximises.

**The trade you'd expect doesn't materialise.** I'd warned that whatever supplies interior cells might also flatten the observable. Here corr(log *V*, log *r*) = +0.14, and median *r* stays above 1,700 — 350× the admission threshold — even in the most neutron-rich bin. Of 24 cells with *V* < 8, all 24 also have *r* > 5. Zero useful-but-invalid. Binding energies are large and mass spectrometry is good, so precision survives far from stability while smoothness does not.

Ceiling, stated plainly in §10.4: the best single cell anywhere in any domain surveyed is ⁵⁴Ca at *V* = 4.74 against a floor of 2. The nuclear chart isn't where the order wins — Proposition 14.1 forbids that — it's a large, well-measured, physically motivated region where the guarantee is cheapest and the alternatives are extrapolating.

§15.4's open question is now sharper and experimental: reaching the floor requires Sₙ → Δ, which means the drip line, so whether measured masses ever get there with *r* still above threshold is a question about the next decade of mass spectrometry.

No — and the paper already contains the proof twice, in sections written before the question existed.

**The index cannot name the quantity.** *V* = 2S̄ₙ/Δ, and both S̄ₙ and Δ are differences of binding energies. §2.2 establishes that a difference of two axes is not of admissible form and cannot be a coordinate; §4.3 tabulates the damage — *h* = *q*−*g* gives 284,858 join failures, *k*−*q* gives 406,400, *e*−*f* gives 266,440. Sₙ has precisely that form. So the quantity governing the open question isn't merely unpredicted by the lattice. It is inexpressible in it. That's a stronger exclusion than Theorem 12.1, which only says lattice quantities cannot exceed the coordinates; this says the relevant quantity is not a lattice quantity at all.

**The method can bracket it, but only after the channel clause — for the fourth time.** Sₙ is not monotone in *A* in any of the nine chains: Ca shows 18 sign reversals in 18 steps, Ti 16 in 16, Cr 18 in 18. Perfect alternation, which is of course the same fact that makes *V* low. Split by parity of *N* and both sub-channels are strictly monotone decreasing in all nine chains. So Rule 1's second clause rescues it, having now done the same work for Sc III 3d, for alkane melting points below C₄, for straight-chain versus branched alkanes, and now for neutron parity — four systems with nothing in common but the need to say what a channel is.

**And then it declines, by Rule 1's first clause.** Extrapolating each even-*N* sub-channel to Sₙ = 0:

| chain | last measured *A* | Sₙ there | Sₙ = 0 at | cells beyond data |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ca | 56 | 2.93 MeV | ~61 | +4 |
| Ti | 58 | 4.59 | ~66 | +8 |
| Ni | 73 | 3.95 | ~92 | +19 |
| Kr | 83 | 7.47 | ~119 | +35 |

The drip line is 4 to 35 cells past the last measured isotope in every chain. Sₙ = 0 is never an interior cell, so the method must extrapolate, which §8's ablation prices at 3.7× in rms. It declines rather than errs — the Ti I outcome, in a different discipline.

So the loop closes on itself. The region where the bracket is most useful is delimited by a quantity the index cannot express and the method refuses to predict. That isn't a gap to patch; it's the thesis applied to its own boundary, and it's the sharpest statement of it in the paper: **the index cannot tell you where indexing is useful.**

That belongs as the closing paragraph of §15.4, replacing the current "question about the next decade of mass spectrometry" framing — which is true but reads as deferral, where this reads as a result. Say the word and I'll write it in.

Written in, split across results and discussion so the numbers sit where a referee expects them.

**New §10.5** carries the data: the total alternation of Sₙ on the bare axis (18 reversals in 18 steps for Ca, 16 in 16 for Ti, 18 in 18 for Cr), the parity split that recovers monotonicity in all nine chains, and the table showing Sₙ = 0 lying 4 to 35 cells beyond the last measured isotope. It ends by naming this as the Ti I outcome in a different discipline — the method declining rather than erring.

**§15.4 now closes with the argument** rather than the deferral. Three moves: *V* = 2S̄ₙ/Δ is a ratio of differences, and differences are the one form §2.1 excludes, with §4.3's failure counts cited as evidence; the method itself declines on Sₙ by its own interiority clause; therefore the index cannot express, and the method cannot predict, where indexing is useful. Stated explicitly as a stronger exclusion than Theorem 12.1, since 12.1 bounds what lattice quantities carry rather than denying that this is one.

**The abstract** now ends on it, and **§15.1** points forward to it as the strongest form of the thesis. Appendix B documents how *B*, σ(*B*), Δ and the drip-line fits were computed, with the fits flagged as range-establishing rather than predictive.

One judgement call worth flagging: I kept the Rule 1 clause-two observation in §10.5 as "four systems sharing no physics, each requiring the same clause." Four instances is enough to be interesting and not enough to be a result. If a referee pushes on it, the defensible claim is that the clause is about channel identity rather than about spectroscopy, not that it generalises.

**The four instances are two mechanisms.** *Contamination* — Sc III 3d, neopentane — breaks monotonicity or throws an isolated outlier, and §8's defect-departure test already catches it. *Superposition* — odd/even alkanes, odd/even *N* — preserves monotonicity exactly and destroys only smoothness. That second one had no test.

**Now it has one.** For a smooth single channel, doubling index spacing halves *V*, so Σ = 2·*V*(split)/*V*(pooled) should sit at 1. It requires nothing but the values.

| sequence | Σ |
|---|---|
| alkane boiling points | 1.04 |
| smooth 1/*n*² control | 1.17 |
| Ca binding energy | 3.66 |
| Ni binding energy | 5.10 |
| Se binding energy | 10.05 |

All nine isotopic chains flag, 3.66 to 10.05. Neither control does. Documented false positive: ΔH_vap at Σ = 9.98, because the series is nearly linear and its second differences sit at the one-decimal rounding floor — so Σ is unreliable when the sequence is straight and the table is coarse. It also only tests period 2.

**And that dissolves the domain.** Every low-*V* case in the paper is an unresolved channel. Split them, as Rule 1 demands, and *V* goes 2.89 → 18.3 for melting points and 12.2 → 31.1 for Ni — while the bracket also widens absolutely, 29.8 → 60.3 K and 18.8 → 36.9 MeV. Both directions wrong, and the rule requires the move. **Corollary 14.2**: approaching Proposition 14.1's floor and obeying Rule 1 have so far been mutually exclusive.

So §15.2's value condition is withdrawn in the same document that proposed it, as item 13 in §15.3. §10.3 and §10.4 now carry forward-pointers marking them as pooled-channel measurements with §10.6 as the correction, and §10.4's neutron-frontier claim is rewritten as the cost of not applying the rule. The §15.4 question becomes: does any sequence stay rough at Σ ≈ 1? We have no example and no argument that one exists — and a proof that none can would close Part III outright.

One thing I'd hold at arm's length: Σ's normalisation assumes locally polynomial behaviour with non-vanishing second derivative, which is exactly what the ΔH_vap failure violates. Before submission that deserves a stated precision floor — something like requiring mean |second difference| to exceed a few times the tabulation granularity — rather than the prose caveat it currently has.

import numpy as np
exec(open('chart.py').read().split('print(f"{')[0])   # CH

def V_of(y):
    y=np.asarray(y,float)
    if len(y)<3: return np.nan,0
    w=np.abs(y[2:]-y[:-2]); e=np.abs(y[2:]-2*y[1:-1]+y[:-2])/2
    return w.sum()/max(e.sum(),1e-30), len(y)-2

print("=== Does resolving the channel destroy the low-V regime? ===\n")
print("A. n-alkane melting points (K), C4-C14")
C=np.arange(4,15); mp=np.array([134.9,143.4,177.8,182.6,216.4,219.7,243.5,247.6,263.6,267.8,279.0])
v,n=V_of(mp);            print(f"   pooled  (C4..C14)      V = {v:6.2f}   ({n} cells)")
v,n=V_of(mp[C%2==0]);    print(f"   even-C sub-channel     V = {v:6.2f}   ({n} cells)")
v,n=V_of(mp[C%2==1]);    print(f"   odd-C  sub-channel     V = {v:6.2f}   ({n} cells)")

print("\nB. nuclear binding energy, nine chains: pooled vs parity-resolved")
print(f"   {'chain':6}{'pooled V':>10}{'even-N V':>11}{'odd-N V':>10}{'ratio':>9}")
tot=[]
for el,(Z,rows) in CH.items():
    A=np.array([r[0] for r in rows],float); B=np.array([r[0]*r[1] for r in rows])
    N=(A-Z).astype(int)
    vp,_=V_of(B); ve,ne=V_of(B[N%2==0]); vo,no=V_of(B[N%2==1])
    sub=np.nanmean([ve,vo]); tot.append((vp,sub))
    print(f"   {el:6}{vp:10.2f}{ve:11.2f}{vo:10.2f}{sub/vp:9.1f}x")

p='v3.md'; s=open(p).read()
def rep(o,n):
    assert s.count(o)==1, f"MISS {o[:60]!r}"
    return s.replace(o,n)

s=rep("""**But Sₙ = 0 is never an interior cell.** Extrapolating each even-*N*
sub-channel:""",
"""**But Sₙ = 0 is never an interior cell.** Extrapolating each even-*N*
sub-channel:""")

# --- new 10.6 ---
s=rep("""Between 4 and 35 cells beyond the last measured isotope in every chain. Rule 1's
first clause forbids extrapolation — priced at 3.7× in rms by the ablation of §8
— so the method declines on Sₙ at the drip line, exactly as it declines on Ti I.""",
"""Between 4 and 35 cells beyond the last measured isotope in every chain. Rule 1's
first clause forbids extrapolation — priced at 3.7× in rms by the ablation of §8
— so the method declines on Sₙ at the drip line, exactly as it declines on Ti I.

### 10.6 The channel clause is one operation, and it has a test

Rule 1's second clause has now been invoked four times in systems sharing no
physics: Sc III 3d, a collapsed orbital among Rydberg members (§8); *n*-alkane
melting points, where the channel begins at C₄ because propane melts below ethane
(§10.3); branched versus straight-chain alkanes in the OH kinetics, 46
monotonicity violations in 251 comparable pairs (§10.2); and neutron parity in
Sₙ (§10.5). Four invocations is a pattern, not a result. This section makes it
one, and the result is not the one we expected.

**Two mechanisms, not four.** The instances divide cleanly. *Contamination* — a
cell that does not belong to the sequence at all, such as Sc III 3d or neopentane
among the *n*-alkanes — breaks monotonicity or produces an isolated local
outlier. *Superposition* — two interleaved sequences treated as one, such as
odd-*C* and even-*C* alkanes, or odd-*N* and even-*N* nuclei — preserves
monotonicity exactly and destroys only smoothness. Contamination is what §8's
defect-departure test already catches. Superposition is not, and it has a
signature of its own.

**A domain-free diagnostic.** For a smooth single channel, doubling the index
spacing *h* multiplies first differences by 2 and second differences by 4, so
*V* ∝ 1/*h* and *V* halves under subsampling by two. Define

> Σ = 2 · *V*(sub-channels) / *V*(pooled).

A single smooth channel gives Σ ≈ 1. Two interleaved channels give Σ ≫ 1, because
splitting removes an alternation that was inflating the pooled second
differences. Σ requires only the values.

| sequence | *V* pooled | *V* split | Σ |
|---|---|---|---|
| *n*-alkane boiling points, C₄–C₁₄ | 49.3 | 25.5 | **1.04** |
| smooth 1/*n*² control | 10.4 | 6.1 | **1.17** |
| Ca binding energy | 11.9 | 21.7 | **3.66** |
| Ni binding energy | 12.2 | 31.1 | **5.10** |
| Se binding energy | 10.9 | 54.7 | **10.05** |
| *n*-alkane melting points, C₄–C₁₄ | 2.89 | 18.3 | **12.69** |

Across all nine isotopic chains Σ runs from 3.66 (Ca) to 10.05 (Se), mean 6.41,
against a single-channel expectation of 1. The diagnostic recovers both
superposition cases and neither control, with no physical input.

**Known failure mode.** *n*-alkane Δ*H*_vap returns Σ = 9.98 and is a false
positive: the series is very nearly linear, so genuine second differences sit at
the quantisation floor of the tabulated values (one decimal place) and the ratio
is dominated by rounding. Σ is unreliable whenever the second differences
approach the reporting precision — that is, whenever *r* is large *and* the
sequence is nearly straight. Σ also tests only period-2 superposition; higher
periods would need the obvious generalisation, which we have not written.

**And now the consequence, which undoes §10.3 and §10.4.** Resolving these
channels does not merely raise *V*; it raises it back into the regime where
interpolation dominates, and it widens the bracket in absolute terms as well:

| | *V* before | *V* after | bracket before | bracket after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| *n*-alkane melting points | 2.89 | 18.3 | 29.8 K | 60.3 K |
| Ni binding energy | 12.2 | 31.1 | 18.8 MeV | 36.9 MeV |

Both quantities move the wrong way, and Rule 1 requires the move. **Every low-*V*
case in this paper is an under-resolved channel**, and once split — as the
method's own first rule demands — *V* returns to 18–55, the range where a
two-point interpolation is an order of magnitude better than the bracket. There
is no observable in anything we have tested for which the bracket competes on
width after Part II's rules are correctly applied.

> **Corollary 14.2 (stated here, proved in §14).** Proposition 14.1's floor of
> *V* = 2 is approached only as one step of a channel vanishes relative to the
> other. In every case we have found where that occurs, the vanishing step is an
> artefact of superposing two channels, and Rule 1 requires the superposition to
> be removed. Approaching the floor and obeying Rule 1 have so far been mutually
> exclusive.

We report this as a result rather than a repair. The channel clause is a single
operation with a test, which is what §10.5 lacked; and applying it removes the
one regime in which the order appeared to contribute more than restatement.""")

open(p,'w').write(s); print("10.6 added")

It became a result, and the result retracts condition (c).

**The four instances are two mechanisms.** *Contamination* — Sc III 3d, neopentane — breaks monotonicity or throws an isolated outlier, and §8's defect-departure test already catches it. *Superposition* — odd/even alkanes, odd/even *N* — preserves monotonicity exactly and destroys only smoothness. That second one had no test.

**Now it has one.** For a smooth single channel, doubling index spacing halves *V*, so Σ = 2·*V*(split)/*V*(pooled) should sit at 1. It requires nothing but the values.

| sequence | Σ |
|---|---|
| alkane boiling points | 1.04 |
| smooth 1/*n*² control | 1.17 |
| Ca binding energy | 3.66 |
| Ni binding energy | 5.10 |
| Se binding energy | 10.05 |
| alkane melting points | 12.69 |

All nine isotopic chains flag, 3.66 to 10.05. Neither control does. Documented false positive: ΔH_vap at Σ = 9.98, because the series is nearly linear and its second differences sit at the one-decimal rounding floor — so Σ is unreliable when the sequence is straight and the table is coarse. It also only tests period 2.

**And that dissolves the domain.** Every low-*V* case in the paper is an unresolved channel. Split them, as Rule 1 demands, and *V* goes 2.89 → 18.3 for melting points and 12.2 → 31.1 for Ni — while the bracket also widens absolutely, 29.8 → 60.3 K and 18.8 → 36.9 MeV. Both directions wrong, and the rule requires the move. **Corollary 14.2**: approaching Proposition 14.1's floor and obeying Rule 1 have so far been mutually exclusive.

So §15.2's value condition is withdrawn in the same document that proposed it, as item 13 in §15.3. §10.3 and §10.4 now carry forward-pointers marking them as pooled-channel measurements with §10.6 as the correction, and §10.4's neutron-frontier claim is rewritten as the cost of not applying the rule. The §15.4 question becomes: does any sequence stay rough at Σ ≈ 1? We have no example and no argument that one exists — and a proof that none can would close Part III outright.

One thing I'd hold at arm's length: Σ's normalisation assumes locally polynomial behaviour with non-vanishing second derivative, which is exactly what the ΔH_vap failure violates. Before submission that deserves a stated precision floor — something like requiring mean |second difference| to exceed a few times the tabulation granularity — rather than the prose caveat it currently has.

Done. The caveat is now a derivation with a threshold and a calibration.

**The floor.** A second difference combines three values with weights (1, −2, 1), so rounding to granularity *q* gives var(*D*) = 6*q*²/12 = *q*²/2, hence sd = *q*/√2. Define κ = ⟨|*D*|⟩/(*q*/√2), evaluated on the pooled sequence *and* each sub-channel separately — splitting quadruples true second differences while leaving rounding noise fixed, so a sub-channel can sit at the floor when the pooled sequence doesn't. That asymmetry is precisely the ΔH_vap failure mode, and it's why the condition can't be stated on the pooled sequence alone.

**Admissibility**: κ ≥ 5 everywhere, and at least three second differences per sub-channel.

**Calibration**, and the reason I'm comfortable with the threshold:

| sequence | κ worst | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| nuclear chains | 2.5–8.7 × 10⁵ | admit |
| Ba I 6s*n*f | ~4 × 10⁴ | admit |
| alkane melting points | 89.6 | admit |
| alkane boiling points | 28.9 | admit |
| alkane ΔH_vap | **1.4** | **reject** |

Any threshold from 3 to 20 partitions this identically — the gap between 1.4 and 28.9 is empty. ΔH_vap fails both clauses independently: sub-channel second differences of 0.0 and ±0.2 kJ/mol against a rounding sd of 0.071, and only two of them per sub-channel.

**Consequences carried through.** Σ = 9.98 for ΔH_vap is withdrawn as item 14 in §15.3, and the sequence is reclassified as one on which Σ cannot be evaluated rather than one showing superposition — which matters, because a false positive left standing would have been evidence against the very claim §10.6 makes. Appendix B records how *q* is read from each source: 0.1 for the alkane tables, 10⁻³ cm⁻¹ for ASD and Curry, and *A* × 10⁻⁴ keV for AME2020, since the tabulated quantity is *B*/*A* to four decimals.

The Ba I row is derived from the paper's existing figures rather than recomputed from levels — second differences of order tens of cm⁻¹ against 10⁻³ cm⁻¹ quotation — and I've flagged it as such in the text. If you want that row on the same footing as the rest it needs the raw 6s*n*f level list run through the same code.

import numpy as np

# Rounding to granularity q gives each value an error of sd q/sqrt(12).

# so var(D_round) = (1+4+1) q^2/12 = q^2/2  ->  sd(D_round) = q/sqrt(2).
# Resolution ratio  kappa = mean|D_measured| / (q/sqrt(2)).
def kappa(y,q):
    y=np.asarray(y,float)
    if len(y)<3: return np.nan,0

    return np.mean(np.abs(D))/(q/np.sqrt(2)), len(D)

    y=np.asarray(y,float); i=np.arange(len(y))
    kp,np_=kappa(y,q); ke,ne=kappa(y[i%2==0],q); ko,no=kappa(y[i%2==1],q)

    print(f"{name:40}{kp:11.1f}{ke:10.1f}{ko:9.1f}{worst:11.1f}   {'admit' if ok else 'REJECT'}")

combines three values with weights (1, −2, 1), so

> var(*D*_round) = (1 + 4 + 1)·*q*²/12 = *q*²/2,  sd(*D*_round) = *q*/√2.

Define the **resolution ratio**

> κ = ⟨|*D*_measured|⟩ / (*q*/√2),

computed on the pooled sequence and on each sub-channel separately, since
splitting quadruples the true second differences while leaving the rounding noise
unchanged — so a sub-channel can sit at the floor when the pooled sequence does
not.

> **Admissibility of Σ.** Σ is reportable only if (i) κ ≥ 5 on the pooled
> sequence *and* on every sub-channel, and (ii) every sub-channel supplies at
> least three second differences, i.e. at least five members. If either fails, the
> second differences are not determined by the data and Σ carries no information
> about channel structure.

**Calibration.** The condition is not tuned; the two populations are separated by
a factor of twenty with nothing in between.

| sequence | *q* | κ pooled | κ worst sub-channel | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ca binding energy | 4.6 × 10⁻³ keV | 8.7 × 10⁵ | 8.7 × 10⁵ | admit |
| Ni binding energy | 6.3 × 10⁻³ keV | 7.0 × 10⁵ | 5.3 × 10⁵ | admit |
| Se binding energy | 7.5 × 10⁻³ keV | 6.8 × 10⁵ | 2.5 × 10⁵ | admit |
| Ba I 6s*n*f levels | 10⁻³ cm⁻¹ | ~4 × 10⁴ | ~4 × 10⁴ | admit |
| *n*-alkane melting points | 0.1 K | 292 | 89.6 | admit |
| *n*-alkane boiling points | 0.1 K | 28.9 | 28.9 | admit |
| *n*-alkane Δ*H*_vap | 0.1 kJ mol⁻¹ | 3.5 | **1.4** | **reject** |

Any threshold between 3 and 20 partitions the table identically. Δ*H*_vap fails
both clauses independently: its sub-channel second differences are 0.0 and ±0.2
kJ mol⁻¹ — zero to two quantisation units against a rounding sd of 0.071 — and
each sub-channel supplies only two of them. Its Σ = 9.98 is therefore withdrawn,
and Δ*H*_vap is recorded as a sequence on which Σ cannot be evaluated rather than
one that shows superposition.

The Ba I entry is derived from the paper's own figures rather than recomputed:
second differences of order tens of cm⁻¹ against levels quoted to 10⁻³ cm⁻¹.

**Remaining limitation.** Σ tests only period-2 interleaving. Three-fold or
incommensurate superposition would need the obvious generalisation, which we have
not written, and the κ condition would carry over to it unchanged.""")

Done. The caveat is now a derivation with a threshold and a calibration.

**The floor.** A second difference combines three values with weights (1, −2, 1), so rounding to granularity *q* gives var(*D*) = 6*q*²/12 = *q*²/2, hence sd = *q*/√2. Define κ = ⟨|*D*|⟩/(*q*/√2), evaluated on the pooled sequence *and* each sub-channel separately — splitting quadruples true second differences while leaving rounding noise fixed, so a sub-channel can sit at the floor when the pooled sequence doesn't. That asymmetry is precisely the ΔH_vap failure mode, and it's why the condition can't be stated on the pooled sequence alone.

**Admissibility**: κ ≥ 5 everywhere, and at least three second differences per sub-channel.

**Calibration**, and the reason I'm comfortable with the threshold:

| sequence | κ worst | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| nuclear chains | 2.5–8.7 × 10⁵ | admit |
| Ba I 6s*n*f | ~4 × 10⁴ | admit |
| alkane melting points | 89.6 | admit |
| alkane boiling points | 28.9 | admit |
| alkane ΔH_vap | **1.4** | **reject** |

Any threshold from 3 to 20 partitions this identically — the gap between 1.4 and 28.9 is empty. ΔH_vap fails both clauses independently: sub-channel second differences of 0.0 and ±0.2 kJ/mol against a rounding sd of 0.071, and only two of them per sub-channel.

**Consequences carried through.** Σ = 9.98 for ΔH_vap is withdrawn as item 14 in §15.3, and the sequence is reclassified as one on which Σ cannot be evaluated rather than one showing superposition — which matters, because a false positive left standing would have been evidence against the very claim §10.6 makes. Appendix B records how *q* is read from each source: 0.1 for the alkane tables, 10⁻³ cm⁻¹ for ASD and Curry, and *A* × 10⁻⁴ keV for AME2020, since the tabulated quantity is *B*/*A* to four decimals.

The Ba I row is derived from the paper's existing figures rather than recomputed from levels — second differences of order tens of cm⁻¹ against 10⁻³ cm⁻¹ quotation — and I've flagged it as such in the text. If you want that row on the same footing as the rest it needs the raw 6s*n*f level list run through the same code.

Got the source — Curry 2004 Table 1, via the NIST public reprint. Running the real levels through the code produced one confirmation and two corrections.

**Confirmation.** The compilation publishes 6s*n*f ³F₂ for *n* = 4–7, 9–12, 17–25. Its gaps are *n* = 8 and 13–16 — exactly §11.2's predicted cells — and your quoted brackets are its own adjacent members: 6s7f at 39 678.176, 6s9f at 40 613.87, 6s12f at 41 251.2, 6s17f at 41 647.85. §11.2 now carries that check.

**Correction 1, and it's a headline.** "Measured to 10⁻³ cm⁻¹" is true of Karlsson and Litzén's low-lying levels. It is not true of the high-*n* members the method actually interpolates: Curry draws those from Armstrong *et al.*, stated typical uncertainty ~0.1 cm⁻¹, and publishes them to between one and three decimal places. Recomputed, the *n* = 17–25 block has **min *r* = 152, not 10⁴–10⁶**. Still thirty times the admission threshold, so nothing about the domain changes — but the margin was overstated by two to three orders of magnitude, and §10.1's "five orders of magnitude inside the plateau" is now a stated range of 10²–10⁶ across the 295 cells. Recorded as withdrawn item 13.

**Correction 2.** The *V* = 19 in §10.3's table divided a five-cell-gap bracket by a six-neighbour Ritz residual — not the comparison *V* is defined as. Computed properly on adjacent neighbours over *n* = 17–25: mean bracket 51.6 cm⁻¹, two-point interpolation error 1.91 cm⁻¹, **V = 27.0**. Item 14.

**And the row you wanted on the same footing.** κ = 540 pooled, 2 025 worst sub-channel, at *q* = 0.01 cm⁻¹ — the coarsest quotation inside the block. Admits. **Σ = 1.03**, sitting alongside the boiling-point control at 1.04, which is a small independent confirmation that a single Rydberg channel is exactly what Part II assumed it to be.

Worth noting the reordering that falls out: Ba I at *r* = 152 is now the *least* comfortably admitted channel in the paper apart from the alkanes — below every nuclear chain by an order of magnitude. The flagship application has the thinnest precision margin of the lot.
